en: This fire is piled in front; the Great Hymn (mahaduktha) is recited above, representing the year.
When Prajāpati was relaxed, his vital essence went upward.
That Prajāpati who was relaxed is the year; and those which were his joints—*Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* 10.1.1.2.
The days and nights fell away from him. That Prajāpati, the year, who fell apart is this very Agni who is now being built up;
and those joints of his, the days and nights, which fell away are these very bricks. Therefore, when he lays down these [bricks], it is for that purpose.
Those very days and nights and joints of his that had fallen apart—those he now restores to him.

Thus, this very sacrificial formula (*yajus*) is piled up here; it is obtained right here. Now, that essence of his which went upward—that is the Great Hymn (*mahad uktham*); that [he now places] in him.
They follow with the *rasa*, the *mṛkṣā*, and the *amā*. As for that *yajus* which goes before it, it goes as one who leads forward;

it is just as when one says, "This one thing of mine was left behind there; I shall fetch it. 10.1.1 [5]. The Adhvaryu takes it with a *graha*; because he takes it, it is called a *graha*. That *yajus* which goes before it—him [the Adhvaryu takes].

They obtain [the year] for a full year; the Udgātṛ places the essence by means of the Mahāvrata. For the Mahāvrata is all these Sāmans; thus he places the essence in it by means of all the Sāmans. In it, the Hotṛ places the essence by means of the Great Hymn (Mahaduktha). For the Great Hymn is all these Ṛcs; thus he places the essence in it by means of all the Ṛcs.
He places it [in the vessel].
When they chant the stotra and when he recites the *anustotra*, then, at the utterance of the *vaṣaṭ* call, he offers this [oblation] into him; thus this essence enters into him.
"This *mahāvrata* chant, once chanted, does not lie still," so they perceive. No.

"This is a great hymn"—thus they behold Agni alone, for Agni is the Self. Therefore, these two, having become *rasa* (essence), enter into him: both the *ṛc* and the *sāman*. Both the *ṛc* and the *sāman* enter into the *yajus*. This Agni is a couple: the first layer and the second, the third and the fourth; then [there is] the fifth.
When fire is deposited in the mind, that is a pair; for this self is indeed a pair.
The thumbs are males, the fingers are females; the ears are males, the eyebrows are females;
the lips are males, the nostrils are females; the teeth are males, the tongue is female—all of them indeed.
He, being a couple, enters this fire, which is a couple, by means of this self that is a couple.

This is the union here. Indeed, even in this way there is a couple; for in this manner, indeed, there is a couple: this speech is one part, and this built-up fire-altar is the other. For by speech the altar is built; and that fire which is placed upon the built altar is the vital breath (*prāṇa*). The vital breath is indeed the male of speech.
Breath is the couple, and speech indeed is this self; now, that which is the breath in the self is the couple.
By means of this self consisting of a couple, he enters into this fire, which is a couple.
This is the absorption here. Indeed, for one who knows these two thus, there is no longer any fear whatsoever of childlessness.
The couple [consists of] the self and Agni; indeed, this self seeks food as its sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
For it has been declared by the Seer: "He who is not our self.
This food, once consumed, becomes twofold: that which is its immortal essence rises upward from the navel, and that which is above the navel [is the immortal part].

It departs with the vital breaths and enters the wind; then that which is mortal passes away from it, but that which is beyond does not pass beyond the navel. Having become these two, it enters this earth—namely, urine and feces. Now, when it enters this earth, it enters that very fire which has been built up.
And when it enters the wind, it enters that fire which is deposited upon the built-up altar. This indeed is the dissolution here. 10.1.2. [1]

Prajāpati desired these worlds. He beheld this self in the form of a bird, Agni; he established it, and by means of it, he attained this world. He beheld a second self in the form of a bird, the Mahāvrata;
he established it, and by means of it, he attained the intermediate space. He [beheld] a third...

Not seeing himself as such, he fashioned that Great Hymn (*mahaduktha*); by means of it, he attained heaven. This world indeed is this piled fire-altar; the intermediate space is the Great Rite (*mahāvrata*); and the sky is the Great Hymn.
Therefore, one should undertake all these together—the fire-altar, the Great Rite, and the Great Hymn—for these worlds are indeed together.
They were created; therefore, Agni is piled first, for he was the first of these worlds to be created—this with respect to the deities (adhidevatam).
Now with respect to the self (adhyātmam): the mind is Agni, the breath is the Mahāvrata, and speech is the Mahaduktha; therefore, these [are so].
One should carry forward all of them together, for mind, breath, and speech go together. In that the fire-altar is built first, it is because the mind is the first of the vital breaths.
The self is the fire-altar; the breath is the Great Vow (mahāvrata); speech is the Great Hymn (mahaduktha). Therefore, one should carry forward all these together.
The self is the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and speech; and since Agni is the first to be piled, the self is indeed the first to come into being for one who comes into being. 10.1.2.
[5] Agni is the head, the *Mahāvrata* is the vital breath, and the *Mahaduktha* is the self; therefore, one should perform all these together, indeed together.
For the head is the vital breath, the self. Now, since the fire-altar is built first, the head indeed is born first of one being born;
therefore, when all these [rites] are performed together, the Great Uktha is manifested as the highest, for the Great Uktha is the self. 10.1.2. [6]
Regarding this they say: "Since all these [sacrifices] are difficult to attain together, how is their attainment?
[The answer is: "In the Jyotiṣṭoma Agniṣṭoma; one should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma Agniṣṭoma itself.
Of this very Jyotiṣṭoma Agniṣṭoma, the Trivṛt Bahiṣpavamāna is the head of the vow.

The two latter *pavamāna*s consist of fifteen and seventeen verses; these are the two wings. The *ājya* of the Hotṛ consists of fifteen verses, the *pṛṣṭha* of seventeen, and the *yajñāyajñiya* of twenty-one; that is the tail. Of those two, the fifteen and the seventeen, there are thirty-two *stotriya* verses; of those, the twenty-five—
Then there is the twenty-fifth, the Self; and those which exceed [the twenty-four], they are the *parimādas*. These are indeed cattle, for the *parimādas* are cattle.
So great indeed is the Mahāvrata; thus, he obtains that very Mahāvrata right here.
Then the Hotṛ recites seven meters, each increasing by four syllables, consisting of single verses, with the Virāj as the eighth. Of these—
There are three eighties and forty-five syllables.

Of these, that which constitutes the eighties is the attainment of the eighties, for by means of the eighties the Great Uktha is proclaimed; then, as for those forty-five, of those, the twenty-five—this is...
The twenty-fifth is the self; where there is the self, that indeed is the head, those are the wings and the tail.
And as for the twenty [verses], that is the insertion. So great indeed is the Mahaduktha; he thus attains this very Mahaduktha right here.
All these [elements] are obtained in the Agniṣṭoma, which is the Jyotiṣṭoma; therefore, indeed—
One should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma Agniṣṭoma.
Prajāpati created living beings; from his upward breaths he created the gods, and from those downward breaths he created mortal creatures.
Then, above the creatures, he created Death as their devourer.
Of that Prajāpati, one half was indeed mortal and one half was immortal.
That which was his mortal part, with that he was afraid of death; being afraid, it entered this [earth], having become twofold: clay and water.
Death said to the gods, "Where has he gone who created us? "Being afraid of you, he has entered this [earth]," they replied.

He said to him, "Let us search for it; let us gather it together, and I shall not harm it. The gods gathered from her what was in the waters, and they gathered those waters; then, what was in her, that clay—having brought both together, the clay and the waters, they made them into bricks. Therefore, these two together constitute the brick.
There is clay and a bow.
These, indeed, were his five mortal bodies: hair, skin, flesh, bone, and marrow; and these are his immortal [bodies]:
mind, speech, breath, sight, and hearing.

He who is that Prajāpati is this very Agni who is being built up. Now, those five mortal bodies of his were these layers of loose earth (*purīṣa-citi*); and those which were immortal were these layers of bricks (*iṣṭakā-citi*).
Those gods said, "Let us make him immortal. By means of those two immortal bodies of his, they [built] this...
Having taken hold of the mortal body, they made it immortal by means of two brick-altars: the *purīṣaciti* first, and likewise the second, the third, and the fourth.
Then, having laid down the fifth layer (*pañcamī citi*), he scatters the loose earth (*purīṣa*); therein [he places] the *vakarṇī* and the *svayamātṛṇā*.

He places the bricks; he sprinkles them with chips of gold; he lays the fire upon them—that is the seventh layer. That is immortality. Thus, by means of these two immortal bodies, they enclosed this mortal body and made it immortal, enclosing the layer of loose earth (purīṣa-citi) between the two layers of bricks. From that indeed...
Prajāpati became immortal; in the same way, the sacrificer, having made this self immortal, becomes immortal.
Those gods did not know whether they had made him complete or not complete, or whether they had left anything out.
While they were thus instructing one another, they saw this *ṛc*: "May Agni, the light-maker; Indra; the divine Bṛhaspati the priest;

and all the gods, being of one mind, protect our sacrifice for prosperity. (10.1.3) Of this [verse], there is indeed a portion addressed to Agni, a portion addressed to Indra, and a portion addressed to the Viśvedevas. Now, as for that portion of it which is addressed to Agni...
Whatever part of this fire was pertaining to Agni, they restored that for him by means of what pertained to Agni; whatever was pertaining to Indra, they restored by means of what pertained to Indra;

whatever was pertaining to the Viśvedevas, they restored by means of what pertained to the Viśvedevas. Thus, right there, they restored it entirely and completely. Therefore, when one stands in worship with this [verse], whatever he might here either over-replenish or fail to replenish—whether knowing or unknowing—they restore it all.
10.1.3. [10] Now, as to why he stands in worship with this [verse]: whatever he here, whether knowing or unknowing, either over-replenishes or fails to replenish...

By means of this [verse], he obtains everything of his that was previously unobtained. It becomes an *anuṣṭubh* containing the word "home" (*dhāman*). For the *anuṣṭubh* is speech, and speech contains the word "home"; by means of speech, he thus obtains whatever of his was unobtained. "One should stand worshipping after having completed the layer provided with loose soil (*purīṣavatī citiḥ*)," so say some; for there it becomes whole and complete. 10.1.3. [11]
Regarding this, they say: "One should worship with [the verse] containing the word 'yaviṣṭha' (the youngest), for that is his beloved abode, namely, 'yaviṣṭha'.

By means of that which is his beloved abode, he thereby obtains whatever of his has not yet been obtained. Since it is a rite for Agni and addressed to Agni, and since the Gāyatrī meter belongs to Agni—Agni being as great as he is, and his measure being as much as it is—it is by just that much that he obtains whatever of his has not yet been obtained."
Furthermore, whatever has not been obtained remains unexpressed; or rather, everything is unexpressed, and by this [verse], he obtains all that of his which was previously unobtained.

"O youngest one, you [give] to the donor"—the significance of this has already been explained. Having constructed a layer (*citi*) provided with loose soil (*purīṣavatī*), he should worship it; for there, indeed, it becomes whole and complete. 10.1.4. [1]

In the beginning, Prajāpati was both of these: the mortal and the immortal. His vital breaths were indeed immortal, while his body was mortal. By means of this rite and this procedure, he made himself one with the undecaying and immortal.
In the same way, the sacrificer becomes both of these: the mortal and the immortal; his vital breaths are indeed immortal.
The body is mortal; by this rite and by this procedure, he makes his self (ātman) entirely ageless and immortal.
He piles the first layer; that indeed is his vital breath (prāṇa). That is immortal, for the vital breath is immortal.
This indeed is their immortal layer. Then he scatters loose soil; that is his marrow.
That, indeed, is mortal, for marrow is mortal. He establishes it upon this immortal [layer], whereby it becomes immortal for him.
(10.1.4) He piles the second layer; that is his downward breath (*apāna*). That, indeed, is immortal, for the downward breath is immortal.
This indeed is the layer of the immortal; this mortal part he encloses on both sides with the immortal, and thereby this part of his becomes immortal.
Then he scatters loose soil (*purīṣa*); that is truly his bone, for bone is mortal; he establishes it upon this immortal foundation, and thereby this part of his becomes immortal. 10.1.4. [4]

He piles the third layer; that indeed becomes his vital breath (vyāna). For that is immortal, since the vital breath is immortal; thus it is the "Immortal Layer. On both sides of this mortal [layer], he encloses it with the immortal; thereby this [mortal part] of his becomes immortal. Then he scatters loose soil; that indeed becomes his sinew for him. For that sinew is mortal.
He establishes this [body] in that immortality; therefore, this [body] of his becomes immortal.
He piles the fourth layer; that indeed is his out-breath (*udāna*). That is truly immortal, for the out-breath is immortal.
This is the "immortal layer" (*amṛta-citi*); he thus encloses this mortal [body] on both sides with the immortal. Therefore, this [body] of his becomes immortal.
Then he scatters the loose soil; that is indeed his flesh, for flesh is mortal.
He establishes it upon this immortal [layer], and thereby this part of him becomes immortal.
He builds the fifth layer; that is his head, for the head is common to all [parts of the body]. That is indeed immortal, for the head is immortal.
This indeed is the layer of the immortal; this mortal part he encloses on both sides with the immortal, and thereby this part of his becomes immortal.
Then he scatters loose soil; that is his fat, for fat is mortal; he establishes it upon that immortal part, and thereby this part of his becomes immortal. 10.1.4. [7]

He piles the sixth layer; that indeed is his speech. For this is truly immortal, since speech is immortal; it is an immortal layer. This mortal [layer] he encloses on both sides with the immortal; thereby this [mortal part] of his becomes immortal.
Then he scatters loose soil; that is indeed his blood and his skin. That, too, is mortal.
For the blood is mortal and the skin is mortal; he establishes that [blood] upon this immortal [skin], and thereby this [blood] of his becomes immortal.
These, indeed, are six layers of bricks and six layers of loose soil; that makes twelve, and twelve months are a year.

The year is Agni; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—by just that much Prajāpati made himself whole, undecaying, and immortal. In the very same way, the sacrificer now makes himself whole, undecaying, and immortal. 10.1.4 [9]

Then, having laid down both the *vikarṇī* and the *svayamātṛṇā*, he sprinkles them with chips of gold and places the fire upon them. That is indeed the form; Prajāpati made that golden form for himself at the very end.
Because it was at the end, therefore this is the final form of his body; therefore they say, "Prajāpati is golden."
In the same way, the sacrificer finally makes for himself a golden form;
because it is at the end, therefore this is the final form of the self. Therefore, whether they know this or not, they say:
"The builder of the fire-altar becomes golden in yonder world. 10.1.4. [10]
Now, regarding this very matter, Śāṇḍilya and Sāptarathavāhani were disputing as teacher and pupil.
"This is his form," said Śāṇḍilya; "the hairs," said Sāptarathavāhani.
Then Śāṇḍilya said: "Form indeed possesses hair, while form is also hairless; it is form alone that this is. That indeed.
It is just as Tāṇḍya said: "When the fire has been piled, it is led forward; after it has been led forward, the fuel-sticks and oblations are offered.
(10.1.4) By means of breath, the gods indeed eat food; Agni is the breath of the gods; therefore, they offer before the gods.
For by means of the out-breath (*prāṇa*) the gods eat food, and by means of the down-breath (*apāna*) humans eat food;

therefore, among humans, food is placed facing downward, for it is by means of the down-breath that humans eat food. Regarding this they say: "One who has built the fire-altar (*agnicit*) should not eat meat, for he who builds the fire-altar becomes the very form of age; he is liable [to become old]."

"Therefore, one who has built the fire-altar (agnicit) should not eat until he has recovered from his affliction. Regarding this, however, one who knows thus may indeed eat at will; for he who builds the fire-altar becomes the very form of Agni. And all this is the food of Agni.
"All this is my food"—thus should one who knows thus understand it. 10.1.4. [14]

Regarding this they say: "What is it that is performed in the fire by which the sacrificer conquers recurrent death? Indeed, he who piles the fire becomes the deity Agni; and Agni is immortality. The gods are prosperity; he attains prosperity. The gods are glory; he indeed becomes glorious—he who knows thus. 10.1.5. [1]

All these are indeed sacrifices: this piled fire-altar (*agni-cita*) is the *Agnyādheya* (the establishment of the sacred fires), when he immolates the victim that constitutes the *Agnyādheya-havīṃṣi* (the oblations of the fire-establishment), when he prepares the fire-pan (*ukhā*), when he undergoes consecration (*dīkṣā*) which is the *Agnihotra*,
and when, being consecrated, he places two fuel-sticks (*samidhau*) on the fire— these are the two *Agnihotra* oblations.
Verily, he establishes [the fires] in the evening and in the morning, for they offer the Agnihotra oblations in the evening and in the morning with the same mantra;

indeed, they offer the Agnihotra oblations with the same mantra. Now, the driving forth of the cattle and the throwing down of the ashes—these two are the New and Full Moon sacrifices (Darśapūrṇamāsa). And as for the piling of the Gārhapatya fire-altar, those are...

The Cāturmāsya sacrifices; then those offerings from the Gārhapatya fire up to the Sarvauṣadha offering; then those animal sacrifices (Paśubandhas) from the Sarvauṣadha offering up to the layers (Citis); whatever Viṣṇukrama steps there are in these sacrifices, those are the Viṣṇukramas; and whatever muttering (Japya) there is, that is the Vātsapra. 10.1.5. [3]
The first layer is the gentle *adhvara* sacrifice; the second is the *rājasūya*, which precedes the *sava*s;

the third is the *vājapeya*; the fourth is the *aśvamedha*; and the fifth is the *agnisava*. That with which he sings around the piled altar with *sāman*s is the *mahāvrata*; and that which is the *udgātṛ*'s recitation there beforehand is the *catasrudriya* and the *vasordhārā*.

Now, as for the Mahaduktha: that which follows the Sāmans and precedes the Vasordhārā is what the Hotṛ recites beforehand; that is it. And as for that which follows the Vasordhārā, those are the Gṛhamedhas. All sacrifices are indeed of this extent; he obtains them all through Agni. 10.1.5. [4]

Now, therefore, regarding the powers of the sacrifices: indeed, in yonder world, one who offers the *agnihotra* eats [the fruit of] it morning and evening; for such is the vigor (*ūrk*) in that sacrifice. One who performs the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices every half-month [eats it] every half-month;

one who performs the *cāturmāsya* sacrifices every four months [eats it] every four months; one who performs the *paśubandha* sacrifice every six months [eats it] every six months; and one who performs the *soma* sacrifice every year [eats it] every year.

Every hundred years, one who has piled the fire-altar may eat according to his desire; yet this [immortality] is not [limited] by those hundreds of years, for it is immortal, infinite, and boundless. For him who knows this thus, this indeed becomes immortal, infinite, and boundless. Of him—

Even that which one might strike as if with a blade of grass, that very thing becomes for him immortal, infinite, and boundless. 10.2.1. Prajāpati desired to go to the heavenly world. Now, all animals are Prajāpati: the human, the horse, the cow, the sheep, and the goat. He was not able [to reach his goal] by means of these forms; he saw this self in the form of birds, namely Agni. That—

He desired to fly up without having folded his wings together and without having spread his feathers; he was not able to do so. Then, having folded his wings together and having spread his feathers, he flew up. Therefore even now, when birds fold their wings together and spread their feathers, they are then able to fly up. 10.2.1 [2]

Or he measures it with his fingers; for man is the sacrifice, and by him all this has been measured. His lowest measure is these fingers; thus he obtains that which is its lowest measure, and by that he measures it. (10.2.1) He measures it with twenty-four fingers; for the Gāyatrī consists of twenty-four syllables.
Agni is of the *gāyatrī* metre; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he measures him out.

He pushes it together by four finger-breadths on both sides from within, and he draws it away by four finger-breadths on both sides from without. As much as he pushes it together, so much he draws it away; thus he makes it neither excessive nor deficient.
He makes [the joints] for the tail in that manner, and likewise for the northern wing.
10.2.1.[5] Then he makes the two joints of the wings; for there are two joints on the wings of a bird.
At one-third [of the length from the root], for at one-third of the wings of a bird the two joints occur. In the middle third, for in the middle third of a bird's wings the joints occur.
The two wings have their joints; it extends four finger-breadths forward and contracts four finger-breadths behind.
As much as it extends, by so much it contracts; thus he neither makes it excessive nor does he make it deficient. 10.2.1 [6]
At that bend he lays down one brick; thus he provides for that single channel which lies alongside the bend of a flying bird.
Then he makes two curves, for the wings of a bird are curved; he makes them exactly four finger-breadths [in width].
He pushes it up from behind by four finger-breadths and draws it together from the front.
As much as he pushes it up, so much does he draw it together; thus he neither exceeds nor makes it deficient.
Then he gives it its highest form; herein this entire Agni is consecrated, and in him the gods—
They bestowed this supreme form upon him; likewise, he bestows this supreme form upon it.
He makes a thousand bricks marked with straight lines—a thousand marked with lines, a thousand marked with lines.
Then, having laid down the fifth layer, he measures out the fire-altar in three parts; he [measures] in the middle third.
He lays down a thousand bricks marked with straight lines; he thereby provides those straight feathers of the bird which extend from the head to the tail.
Then he lays down a thousand bricks marked with curved lines on the right side; he thereby provides those curved feathers of the bird which are on the right side.
He makes those curved feathers;

10.2.1.[11] Then he lays down a thousand [feathers] drawn out on the north side; thus he makes those curved feathers which are these on the north side of the bird. With a thousand—verily, a thousand is everything.

In this [fire-altar], he bestows this supreme form upon it in its entirety; by means of three thousand [bricks], Agni is threefold (trivṛt). As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—by that much alone he bestows this supreme form upon him. 10.2.2. [1]

Those seven persons whom they indeed made into one person became Prajāpati; he created offspring. Having created offspring, he ascended upwards and went to that world where this sun now shines. At that time, there was no other here worthy of sacrifice besides him. Therefore, the gods resolved to worship him by means of the sacrifice itself. 10.2.2. [2]

Therefore, this was declared by the Seer: "By means of sacrifice, the gods sacrificed to the sacrifice. For by means of sacrifice the gods did indeed sacrifice to that sacrifice; "those were the first ordinances"—for those ordinances were indeed performed first; "they, the mighty ones, attained the firmament"—the firmament is indeed the heavenly world, [and] the gods.

"Those gods, your greatnesses, attained the heavenly world, who sacrificed that sacrifice"—this means those very ones. "Where the ancient Sādhyas, the gods, abide"—the Sādhyas, indeed, are the vital breaths (*prāṇa*); they first accomplished this [sacrifice] in this manner, desiring to become this very thing; and even now, they continue to accomplish it.

"Then this other [thing] became worthy of sacrifice, the being of the immortal world. Thus he said: "Indeed, this other [thing] became worthy of sacrifice—whatever is immortal. 10.2.2. [4] "The fair-winged, soaring one of Savitṛ was born first; he indeed follows his law. Prajāpati, indeed, is [that].
"This is Suparṇa Garutman, Savitṛ; Prajāpati follows his law"—thus it is said.
He indeed consists of seven persons, for this person consists of seven persons: four are the self and three are the wings and tail;
for of that person, four are the self and three are the wings and tail.
Or rather, he measures it with a man with upstretched arms; for the sacrifice is indeed a man, and by him all this has been measured.

This [measure] of his is the supreme measure, namely when the arms are upstretched; thus he obtains that which is his supreme measure, and by means of that he measures it out. In that regard, what space remains when he is stepped upon by the forefoot, that he obtains by means of the *pariśrit* bricks.
Therefore, one should dig the trenches for the *pariśrit* enclosing stones using only the outer line.
Then he places two *aratni* measures on the two wings; thus he bestows strength upon the wings.
The wings are indeed the arms, and by means of the arms food is eaten; he thus provides space for food. That which [he does] regarding the two wings and the *aratnis*—
He places [the brick] at a distance of one cubit (*aratni*), for food is eaten from a distance of one cubit.
Then he places it at a span (*vitasti*) in the tail; he thereby bestows vigor upon the foundation, for the tail is indeed the foundation and the span is the hand;
by means of the hand, food is eaten. He thus provides that space for the sake of food. As for why [he places it] in the tail...

He places it at a span's distance; he thereby establishes it in food. As for the fact that he places it there at a smaller distance, he thereby establishes it in food indeed. Moreover, this [world] is measured by just so much, and this is just so much;
thus, when he measures it in this way, it is for the sake of attaining this very thing. 10.2.3. [1]

Or rather, this altar is the measure of the sevenfold altar. Having settled upon the sacrificial ground for the gods, having entered the hall of the wives by the eastern door, and having dug up the site for the Gārhapatya fire, he sprinkles it with water. From the dug-up site of the Gārhapatya, he strides seven steps forward toward the east; from there, he measures a fathom (vyāma) toward the east, and in the middle of that—
Having dug up the ground for the Āhavanīya fire, he sprinkles it with water. From the eastern half of the *vyāma*, he strides three steps forward;
that is the edge of the altar (*vedi*). These strides, measuring eleven *vyāmas* between the edge of the altar and the Gārhapatya fire, consist of eleven syllables.
The Triṣṭubh is a thunderbolt; the Triṣṭubh is vigor. By means of that very thunderbolt and that vigor, the sacrificer repels the Rakṣases and the destroyers from the front of the sacrifice.
This is the womb of the altar; from this very womb the gods generated the altar, and that which is this fathom-long space is it.
The Gārhapatya is the womb; from this very womb the gods generated the Gārhapatya, and from the Gārhapatya the Āhavanīya.
He measures out the Vedi thirty-six steps long toward the east and thirty steps across at the back.

Twenty-four steps in front—thus it is ninety; this is the altar measuring ninety steps, upon which he arranges the sevenfold fire-altar. Regarding this they say: "How does this sevenfold [altar] correspond to this altar? There are indeed ten vital breaths in a person.

The vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are four limbs, and the self (*ātman*) is fifteen; thus it is in the second [set], and thus in the third. Among these six persons, there are ninety. Now, one person exceeds [this number]. Man is indeed fivefold (*pāṅkta*): hair, skin, flesh, bone, and marrow. This altar (*vedi*) is fivefold: the four quarters and the self as the fifth. Thus this sevenfold [altar] is completed by means of this fivefold altar. 10.2.3. [6]
Now, some, intending to construct the northern enclosure, increase these steps and this fathom, saying, "We are increasing the womb. One should not do so;
for the womb does not expand after the embryo has been born; rather, it remains exactly as large as the embryo is within the womb.
The womb grows to this extent; indeed, this is the full measure of the growth of the embryo.

Those who act in that manner cause their father Prajāpati to fall from his perfection; having sacrificed thus, they become worse off, for they cause their father Prajāpati to fall from his perfection. This [growth] is as much as this...

The altar of the sevenfold [fire-altar] is of such a size; he measures out the altar for the one hundred and fourfold [fire-altar] fourteen times. 10.2.3.[8] Then he measures a cord thirty-six steps long; he folds it into seven parts.
Of this, he lays down three parts toward the east and leaves out four. 10.2.3.[9]
Then he measures one of thirty steps; he contracts it into seven parts and lays down three of its parts at the back, leaving four aside. 10.2.3.
[10] Then he measures one of twenty-four steps; he contracts it into seven parts, and of that—

He lays down three parts in front and leaves out four; such is the measurement of the altar. Now, as for the proportions of the fire-altar: there are twenty-eight man-lengths extending eastward and twenty-eight across; that is the body. The right wing consists of fourteen man-lengths, the left wing fourteen, and the tail fourteen. There are fourteen cubits on the south side.
He lays down the wings; there are fourteen spans on each side, and fourteen cubits for the tail—this indeed is the measure of ninety-eight men of full stature.
Then he measures a cord three *puruṣas* long and folds it into seven parts; from that [cord], four...
He places the portions within himself; he places three in the wings and the tail.
10.2.3.[13] Then he measures out one [line] a cubit long; he divides it into seven parts. Of this, he places three parts on the right wing, three on the left, and leaves four remaining. 10.2.3.[14]

Then he measures it out to the extent of a span; he folds it into seven parts and lays down three parts on the back, leaving four aside. In this way, this [altar] of one hundred and onefold [bricks] is completed by means of this sacrificial ground.
Regarding this they say: "Since thirteen men exceed [the measure], how is it that these do not fall away from the completion? As for those...
The perfection of this seventh person is indeed the perfection of all these.
Now they say: Prajāpati, having fashioned himself, filled whatever was deficient in him with these; thus he became complete.
