He who establishes a form exceeding the hundred-and-onefold establishes it beyond his father Prajāpati;
he indeed dismembers that father Prajāpati, and having sacrificed, he becomes worse off, just as one who has harmed a superior.
But he who establishes a form exceeding the hundred-and-onefold falls outside of this entire universe, for this whole world is the hundred-and-onefold.
Therefore, Prajāpati should first construct it as having seven parts, and then one more each time up to one hundred and one parts; however, he should not exceed one hundred and one parts.
For he does not dismember this father Prajāpati, nor does anything of him fall outside of himself. 10.2.4. [1]
Prajāpati is indeed the year, and Agni is all desires. This Prajāpati, the year, desired: "May I build up Agni, all desires, as my own self. He divided himself into one hundred and one parts;
having divided himself into one hundred and one parts, he built up Agni, all desires, as his own self. He...

All desires were contained therein; therefore, no desire existed outside of it. Hence they say, "The year is all desires," for indeed, there is no desire whatsoever outside of the year. In the same way, the sacrificer, having divided himself into one hundred and one parts, [establishes] the fire...
He accumulates all desires within himself; he becomes all desires, and therefore no desire exists outside of him.
That which is the year is this very sun; it is this one hundred and one-fold [sacrifice], whose rays are its one hundred parts.

This very one which shines here is the hundred-and-first, established upon all this; in the same way, the sacrificer, having divided himself into a hundred-and-one parts, becomes established upon all this. Now, indeed, that which is of a hundred-and-onefold form attains to the sevenfold; for yonder sun is distributed in a hundred-and-one ways.

He is established in the seven worlds of the gods. Indeed, there are seven worlds of the gods: the four quarters, these three worlds—these indeed are the seven worlds of the gods; in them he is established. In the same way, the sacrificer, having divided himself into one hundred and one parts, becomes established in the seven worlds of the gods. 10.2.4 [5]

Or rather, as to why that which is of one hundred and one kinds attains to the sevenfold: for yonder sun is distributed in a hundred and one ways—he is established in the seven seasons, in the seven stomas, in the seven pṛṣṭhas, in the seven meters, in the seven vital breaths, and in the seven directions;
in the very same way, the sacrificer here establishes himself in a hundred and one ways.
Having arranged all this, he establishes himself therein.

Furthermore, as to why that which is of one hundred and onefold form attains to the sevenfold form: that sun is indeed distributed in one hundred and one ways, and it is established upon the seven-syllabled Brahman. The Brahman is indeed seven-syllabled: "Ṛk" is one syllable, "Yajuḥ" is [another].
"Two *sāma*s"—these two; and what is other than these is indeed Brahman. Brahman consists of two syllables.
This entire [sevenfold] Brahman consists of seven syllables. Upon this [Brahman] he is established.
In the same way, the sacrificer, having divided himself into one hundred and one parts, becomes established upon the seven-syllabled Brahman. 10.2.4. [7]
Therefore they enclose it with seven [layers] each; thus the one hundred and one-fold becomes the sevenfold, or rather, the sevenfold becomes the one hundred and one-fold.
In the beginning, Prajāpati was created as sevenfold; he [divided] this self into one hundred and one parts.

He saw that among living beings there were fifty bricks and fifty sacrificial formulas; the settling and the *sūdadohas* verses made up one hundred and one. Having settled that which is common [to all], he consecrates it with the *sūdadohas*.
By means of this self consisting of one hundred and one parts, he won this victory and attained this pre-eminence.

In the same way, by means of this one-hundred-and-one-fold self, the sacrificer wins this victory and attains this distinction; thus the sevenfold becomes the one-hundred-and-one-fold. That which is the one-hundred-and-one-fold is the sevenfold, and that which is the sevenfold is the one-hundred-and-one-fold. Such is the rule. 10.2.5. [1]

Now, therefore, regarding the piling itself: he piles [the altar] between the two Upasad days. For the gods were afraid, thinking, "Lest the Rakṣases, the destroyers, should slay this [altar] of ours here. They saw these fortresses, namely the Upasads; these worlds are indeed the fortresses.
They entered them, and having entered them, they prepared this self (the altar) in a place free from danger and destruction.

In the same way, the sacrificer, having entered these fortresses, prepares this self in a state free from fear and free from destructive spirits. Furthermore, as to why he piles [the altar] between the two *upasad* offerings: the gods were indeed afraid, thinking, "Lest the *rakṣases*, the destroyers, should strike down this [altar] of ours here"; they saw these *vajras*, for the *upasads* are indeed *vajras*, and they took refuge in them.

Having sought refuge in them for safety and freedom from harm, they fashioned this self; in the same way, the sacrificer now, having sought refuge in these thunderbolts for safety and freedom from harm, fashions this self.
This, indeed, is the austerity in the sacrifice that constitutes the *upasads*; for the *upasads* are austerity, and it is upon that austerity that [the fire-altar] is built.
Therefore, that heat is indeed accumulated; for as long as they perform with the *upasads*, so long do they perform with the *pravargya*.
They perform with the *upasads* for a year, and with the *pravargya* for a year.
The *upasads* are the days and nights, and the *pravargya* is the sun; thus, they place that sun within the days and nights.
He establishes it; therefore, this [sacrifice] is established in the days and nights.
Now, if there are twenty-four [days], for indeed there are twenty-four half-months, and the Upasads are the half-months while the Pravargya is Āditya;
he thus establishes that Āditya in the half-months. Therefore, this [sacrifice] is established in the half-months.
[6] Now, if there are twelve [days], the months are indeed twelve; the Upasads are the months, and the Pravargya is the sun. Thus, he establishes that sun in the months;
therefore, it is established in the months. [7] Therefore, this [sun] is established in the months.
Now, if there are six [Upasad days], for the seasons are six; the Upasads are the seasons and the Pravargya is the sun. Thus, he establishes that sun in the seasons;

therefore, this [sun] is established in the seasons. Now, if there are three [Upasad days], for these worlds are three; the Upasads are these worlds and the Pravargya is the sun. Thus, he establishes that...
He thereby establishes the sun in these worlds; therefore, it is established in these worlds.

Now, therefore, follows the investigation of the layers (*citi*) and the fillings (*purīṣa*): one month is the first layer, one month is the filling; such is the desire in the spring season. Whatever desire there is in the spring season, that—
He piles all that together as his self.

(10.2.5.10) For one month it is the second layer, for one month the loose earth; such is the desire in the summer season. Whatever desire there is in the summer season, all that he piles together as his self. (10.2.5.11)

A month of *tṛtīyā* bricks, a month of *purīṣa*—this much is the desire in the rainy season; thus, whatever desire there is in the rainy season, all that he accumulates within himself. A month of *caturthī* bricks, a month of *purīṣa*—this much is the desire in the autumn season; thus, whatever desire there is in the autumn season...
Desire collects all that for him as his very self. 10.2.5.

[13] Now, for the fifth layer, he first lays down the *asapatnā* and *virāj* bricks; he lays them down one by one every day, and those *stomabhāgā* bricks he settles all at once. He pronounces the *sūdadohas* formula over them all at once, and he remains silent for a month.

They bring the *stomabhāga* and the *purīṣa*; such is the desire in the winter season. Thus, whatever desire there is in the winter season, all that he builds up for himself. For one month [is the *ṣaṣṭhī*], for one month the *purīṣa*; such is the desire in the dewy season (*śiśira*). Thus, whatever desire there is in the dewy season—
Desire collects all that for itself as its own body; for such is the extent of desire in twelve months and in six seasons.
Thus, whatever desire there is in twelve months and in six seasons, all that it collects for itself as its own body. 10.2.5 [15]

Now, three days pass by: the day on which he offers the Śatarudriya, the day of the Upavasatha, and the day of the pressing. In those days, when they perform the Upasad rites, these constitute the days and nights of that month.
Then, by means of the Pravargya, he establishes the Āditya in that season; such indeed is the extent within the thirteen [months].

The desire that exists in seven months and seven seasons—that entire desire which exists in thirteen months and seven seasons—he thereby gathers into himself. He should be consecrated for a year; for the year is everything, and the one hundred and one-fold sacrifice is everything; thus, by means of everything, he attains everything.
He obtains all that if he is unable [to perform it for] a year; he should sacrifice with the Viśvajit, an Atirātra with all the Pṛṣṭhas.
In that sacrifice, he should give away his entire property (*sarvavedasa*). The Viśvajit, the Atirātra with all the Pṛṣṭhas, is indeed everything;
the entire property is everything; the one hundred and one-fold [sacrifice] is everything. By means of everything, he thus obtains everything. 10.2.6.1.
Prajāpati is indeed the year, consisting of one hundred and one forms. Its forms are the days and nights, the half-months, the months, and the seasons.
There are sixty days and nights in a month; thus, in a year, the days and nights are completed.
There are twenty-four half-months, thirteen months, and three seasons; these constitute the hundred forms of the year. Prajāpati is the year.
This is the one hundred and first mode (vidhā).
[10.2.6.2] It is sevenfold by means of the seasons: the six seasons and the year as the seventh mode. Of this very year, that which shines yonder is the splendor; its rays are the hundred modes.

The hundred-and-first mode is the mandala itself. 10.2.6.[3] It is sevenfold by means of the directions: those rays which are in the eastern direction constitute one mode; those in the southern, one; those in the western, one; those in the northern, one; those in the upward direction, one; and those in the downward direction, one—the mandala itself.

The seventh mode: 10.2.6.[4] Before this [fire], there is the world called Kāmapra; Kāmapra is indeed immortality (amṛta). That which is behind it is immortality itself, which is that flame which shines here. 10.2.6.[5]

This is indeed a manifold and wonderful gift; Savitṛ distributes it among these creatures, even unto the plants and the trees. Yet he gives more to some and less to others. Those to whom he gives more live longer, while those to whom he gives less [live shorter].

The younger ones (kanīyastāḥ) 10.2.6. [6]. This very thing is expressed by a Ṛgvedic verse: "We invoke Savitṛ, the distributor of wonderful wealth and bounty, who beholds men. All this is long life; for that is indeed endless which they call "long" (dīrgha). Ta.

"May there be life; may there be all life here"—this is what she says when she speaks while looking on, meaning "This world is yours; let it be yours. This very thing is to be attained either by means of the one-hundred-and-one-fold sacrifice or by a hundred-year lifespan.
He who ordains the one-hundred-and-one-fold sacrifice, or he who lives for a hundred years—he indeed attains this immortality.

Therefore, those who know this and those who do not say, "A hundred thousand worlds. For this reason, one should not depart before the end of one's lifespan according to one's own desire; for these indeed are the worlds that are not [attained by others]: namely, days and nights, half-months, months, seasons, and the year.
Now, those who depart when there are fewer than twenty years remaining are joined with the worlds that are the days and nights;
then those who depart when there are fewer than forty years remaining are joined with the half-months;

then those who depart when there are fewer than sixty years remaining are joined with the months; and then those who depart when there are fewer than eighty years remaining are joined with the seasons.
Now, those who live for more than eighty years but less than a hundred, and those who live for exactly a hundred years, or even longer—they indeed attain this immortality.
For by many sacrifices, one day and one night are measured; he who ordains the one-hundred-and-one-fold [sacrifice], he—
Or he lives for a hundred years; he indeed attains this most truly. He who maintains this [altar] for a year ordains the one-hundred-and-one-fold [sacrifice];

therefore, one should pile it only after it has been maintained for a year. This is with respect to the deities (adhidevatam). Now, with respect to the sacrifice (adhiyajñam): when he measures out those one hundred and one men with upraised arms, that is the one-hundred-and-one-fold division. That [is the altar].
It is sevenfold by means of the layers (*cita*); six layers consist of the six seasons, and Agni himself is the seventh layer.
10.2.6.[11] Furthermore, he is indeed one hundred and one-fold by means of bricks: those which are the first fifty bricks and those which are the last [fifty] make a hundred divisions;
then, those bricks which are placed between these two constitute the one-hundred-and-first division. 10.2.6.[12]

That very sacrifice is the splendor of the *yajus*; the hundredfold sacrifice consists of those fifty *yajus* formulas which are first and those which are last—these constitute the hundred forms; and those *yajus* formulas which are performed between them constitute the one hundred and first form.
Thus, the sevenfold becomes the hundredfold. Whatever desire there is for a hundred thousand...
In the one-hundred-and-one-fold [sacrifice], there are seven [elements]; indeed, he who knows thus attains that very [sacrifice] by means of the sevenfold [elements].
10.2.6.[13] In this very way, all sacrifices from the *agnihotra* onwards consist of one hundred and one parts, [divided] by *ṛc*s, *yajus*s, words, and syllables.

"By means of rituals and chants, that which is desired in the hundred-thousandfold [sacrifice], that which is in the one-hundred-and-one-fold, and that which is in the seven-fold—by sacrifice after sacrifice, indeed, he who knows thus attains that very thing. Thus far with respect to the sacrifice (adhiyajña).
Now with respect to the self (adhyātma): these five fingers, each four-jointed; the two wrists; the arm; and the shoulder-blade.
And the axle is the twenty-fifth; thus these other limbs [make up] those hundred modes. The Self alone is the one hundred and first mode, declared for the sake of the sevenfold nature.
That very same [Self] is the vital heat of breath, the hundred-and-one-fold breath, for the breath is in every single limb. He who...

The desire that exists in the hundred-and-one-fold sacrifice, that which exists in the sevenfold, and that which exists in all sacrifices—one who knows thus obtains that very [desire] through knowledge alone; for he knows himself as endowed with all sacrifices. 10.2.6. [16]

These three are fivefold: the year, Agni, and the person. Their fivefold forms are food, drink, prosperity, light, and immortality. That which is food in the year is food; that which is water is drink; the night itself is prosperity, for on the night of prosperity all beings rest.
"They dwell together with the light of day; the sun is the immortal"—this is with respect to the deities (adhidevatam).
Now, with respect to the sacrifice (adhiyajñam): that food which is placed upon the fire is the food; the waters are the drink;
the enclosing stones (*pariśrit*) are prosperity (*śrī*), for they are the form of the nights; the *yajus*-bearing bricks are the light, for they are the form of the days; Agni is the immortal.
"That indeed is the form of the sun"—this is with reference to the sacrifice (adhiyajña).

Now, with reference to the self (adhyātma): that which is food in a person is [the sacrificial] food; the waters are the drink; the bones are beauty (*śrī*), for that is the form of the enclosing bricks (*pariśrit*);
the marrow is light (*jyotis*), for that is the form of the *yajuṣmatī* bricks; the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is immortality (*amṛta*), for that is the form of Agni.
"Form is breath, fire is breath, and immortality is breath," so they say.

From food, indeed, hunger ceases; from drink, thirst; from prosperity, evil; from light, darkness; and from immortality, death. Verily, all these turn away from him who knows this; he conquers recurrent death and attains a full lifespan.
Therefore, one should worship this as "the immortal" in the world beyond, and as "life" here on earth. Some, however, worship it as "breath," saying, "Breath is Agni;
breath is the immortal. One should not know it thus. For that which is breath is indeed unstable. Indeed, it is also stated in a Yajus verse: "I loosen you from the midst of life."
Therefore, one should meditate upon this as "the immortal" in the world beyond, and as "life" here on earth; thus, indeed, one attains a full span of life.
10.3.1. [1] Breath is the Gāyatrī; sight is the Uṣṇih; speech is the Anuṣṭubh; mind is the Bṛhatī; hearing is the Paṅkti;
that which is this generative breath is the Triṣṭubh; and that which is this downward breath is the Jagatī. These, then, are the seven.
The *candāṃsi* (metrical hymns) are made fourfold more in the fire-altar.
"The *gāyatrī* is breath"—thus, whatever is the greatness and whatever is the vigor of breath, that is this thousandfold [altar].
This is indeed the vigor of breath; for if the breath were to depart from him while he is building it, then this fire-altar would not [be completed].
By this very form it is piled; this becomes a thousand *gāyatrīs* when built up.
"The *uṣṇih* is the eye"—thus, whatever greatness and whatever vigor belongs to the eye, that is this thousand;
this is indeed the vigor of the eye, for if the eye were to depart from him while he is building, then this fire-altar would not [be completed].
By this very form of his, it would be piled; this *uṣṇih* becomes piled as a thousandfold.
"The *anuṣṭubh* is speech"—thus, whatever is the greatness and whatever is the power of speech, that is this thousandfold; this is indeed the power of speech.
For if speech were to depart from him while he is piling, then by that very fact this fire-altar would not be piled; [it is piled] by this very form of his.
This [altar] is built up with a thousand *anuṣṭubh* verses.
"The mind is the *bṛhatī*," it is said; thus, whatever is the greatness and the power of the mind, that is this thousand.
This is indeed the power of the mind: for if the mind of one who is building were to depart, then this fire-altar would not be built. By this very [power], his...
In form, this [altar] becomes a thousandfold when piled with *bṛhatī* verses.
(10.3.1.6) The ear is the *paṅkti*. Thus, whatever is the greatness and the power of the ear, that is this thousandfold [altar].
This is indeed the power of the ear; for if the ear were to depart from him while he is piling it, then this fire-altar would not [be completed].
By this very form it is piled; this [altar], when built up, consists of a thousand *paṅkti* verses.

That which is this procreative breath—that is the *triṣṭubh*. Thus, whatever is the greatness and the vigor of this breath, that is this thousand. This is indeed the vigor of this very breath, for while he is building it, this breath [remains].
It would then become agitated; thus this fire would not be piled. By means of this very form, this [fire] becomes piled with a thousand *triṣṭubh* verses.
Now, that which is this downward breath—that is the *jagatī*. Whatever greatness and whatever vigor belongs to this breath—this is it.

This thousandfold power belongs to this very breath; for if this breath were to depart from him while he is building, then this fire-altar would not be built. By means of this very form, this [altar], when completed, consists of a thousand *jagatī* verses.

Now, these seven meters increase by four syllables each and are established one upon another; likewise, these seven vital breaths in a person are established one upon another. Therefore, however much of the collection of meters one who knows this recites, for him that becomes as if recited, praised, chanted, or placed [as an oblation], meter by meter. 10.3.2. [1]

Regarding this they say: "What is the metre, what is the deity of the head of Agni? The *gāyatrī* is the metre, Agni is the deity; [this is] the head. (10.3.2.2) "What is the metre, what is the deity of the neck? The *uṣṇih* is the metre, Savitṛ is the deity; [these are] the necks. (10.3.2.3) "What is the metre, what is the deity of the spine? The *bṛhatī* is the metre, Bṛhaspati is the deity; [this is] the spine. (10.3.2.4)
What is the metre, and what is the deity, of the two wings? The Bṛhat and Rathantara [Sāmans] are the metre; Heaven and Earth are the deities of the two wings.
10.3.2.[5] What is the metre, and what is the deity, of the middle? The Triṣṭubh is the metre; Indra is the deity of the middle.
10.3.2.[6] What is the metre, and what is the deity, of the two hips? The Jagatī is the metre; Āditya is the deity of the two hips. 10.3.2.[7]
"What is the meter, what is the deity, from which this semen is emitted through the vital breath? "The *aticandāḥ* is the meter;
Prajāpati is the deity. 10.3.2.[8] "What is the meter, what is the deity, of this downward vital breath? "The *yajñāyajñīya* is the meter; Vaiśvānara is the deity. 10.3.2.[9]
What is the metre, what is the deity for the thighs? The *anuṣṭubh* is the metre, the Viśvedevas are the deity for the thighs.
10.3.2.[10] What is the metre, what is the deity for the knees? The *paṅkti* is the metre, the Maruts are the deity for the knees.
10.3.2.[11] What is the metre, what is the deity for the feet? The *dvipadā* is the metre, Viṣṇu is the deity for the feet. 10.3.2.[12]

"What is the metre? What is the deity? The vital breaths. "The *vicchandāḥ* is the metre; Vāyu is the deity; the vital breaths [are the bricks]. "What is the metre? What is the deity? The deficient ones. "The *nyūnākṣarā* is the metre; the waters are the deity; the deficient ones [are the bricks].
This is indeed the knowledge of the Self (*ātmavidyā*). Consisting of this very [Self], he attains these deities and this Self; for here there is nothing else.
There is a blessing regarding the world of the living.
10.3.3.[1] A wise man of the Śataparna clan approached Mahāśāla Jābāla and said to him, "Knowing what have you come to me?
"I know Agni," he replied. "Which Agni do you know? "Speech. "What does one who knows that Agni [know]?"

"He becomes eloquent," he said; "speech does not desert him. "Do you know Agni? he asked. "Knowing what did you approach me? "I know Agni. "Which Agni do you know? "The eye. "What does he become who knows that Agni? "He becomes possessed of sight," he said; "sight does not desert him."
"The eye departs," [he said]. "Do you know Agni? he asked. "Knowing what, have you come here to me? "I know Agni. "Which Agni do you know? "The mind (manas).
"What becomes of him who knows that Agni? "He becomes possessed of a mind," he replied. "The mind does not abandon him."
"He leaves behind," [it is said]. "Do you know Agni? he asked. "Knowing what have you come to me as a student?
"I know Agni. "Which Agni do you know? "The ear. "What becomes of him who knows that Agni? "He becomes possessed of hearing," he replied. "It does not [fail him]."
"He loses his hearing," [he said].
"Do you know Agni? he asked. "Knowing what, have you come here to me as a pupil? "I know Agni. "Which Agni do you know?
"I know that Agni who is all this. When this was said, [the other] descended [from his seat] and said, "Teach me that Agni, sir!"

He said: "That fire is indeed the vital breath (prāṇa). When a person sleeps, then speech merges into the vital breath, sight merges into the vital breath, mind merges into the vital breath, and hearing merges into the vital breath. When he awakens, they are born again from the vital breath alone. This is with reference to the self (adhyātma). 10.3.3 [7]

Now, with respect to the deities: that which is speech is indeed Agni; that which is sight is yonder sun, Āditya; that which is mind is this moon; that which is hearing is the quarters; and that which is breath is this very wind that blows here. 10.3.3. [8]
When fire goes out, it then blows along with the wind; therefore they say of it, "It has blown out," for it indeed blows along with the wind.
When the sun sets, it enters the wind; the moon enters the wind; in the wind the quarters are established;
from the wind alone they are born again. When one who knows this departs from this world—
By speech alone one enters Agni; by sight, the Sun; by mind, the Moon; by hearing, the Quarters; and by breath, Vāyu.
Having become composed of these very things, he moves about having become whichever of these deities he desires.
Śvetaketu Āruṇeya was about to perform a sacrifice. His father said to him, "Which priests have you chosen? He replied, "This one..."

"Is this indeed the Vaiśvāvasavya Hotṛ? He asked him: "O Brāhmaṇa Vaiśvāvasavya, do you know the four great things? "I know them, sir," he replied. "Do you know the four greater-than-great things? "I know them, sir," he replied. "Do you know the four vows? "I know them, sir," he replied. "Do you know the four [things] of the vows..."
"Do you know the *vratas*? "I know them, sir," he replied. "Do you know the four *kyās*? "I know them, sir," he replied.

"Do you know the four *kyās* of the *kyās*? "I know them, sir," he replied. "Do you know the four *arkas*? "I know them, sir," he replied. "Do you know the four *arkas* of the *arkas*? "I know them, sir," he replied. (10.3.4)

"Do you know the *arka*?"—"Now, surely you will tell us, sir. "Do you know the two *arkaparṇa* leaves?"—"Now, surely you will tell us, sir. "Do you know the two *arkapuṣpa* flowers?"—"Now, surely you will tell us, sir.
"Do you know the two *arkakośyā* pods?"—"Now, surely you will tell us, sir. "Do you know the two *arkasamudga* boxes?"—"Now, surely you will tell us, sir."
"If you will tell us, sir, do you know the *arkadhānā*s?"—"Yes.
"If you will tell us, sir, do you know the *arkāṣṭhīlā*?"—"Yes. "If you will tell us, sir, do you know the root of the *arka*?"—"Yes.
"If you will tell us, sir... 10.3.4 [4]

Now, as for what he said: "You know the four great ones; you know the four great among the great. Fire is great; the great among that great one are the herbs and the trees, for they are its food. Wind is great; the great among that great one are the waters, for they are its food. The sun... [is great].
Of that great one, the moon is the great greatness, for that is his food; man is the great greatness of that great one, for he is his food;
cattle are the great greatness of that great one, for they are his food. These indeed are the four great things;
these are the four great things of the great. These indeed are the four vows; these are the four vows of vows. These indeed are the four.

What are these four quarters? What are these four Arka trees? These four are the Arka trees of the Arkas. Now, as for what he said: "Do you know the Arka?"—he was indeed speaking of the person. "Do you know the two Arka leaves?"—he was indeed speaking of the ears. "Do you know the two Arka flowers?"—he was indeed speaking of the eyes. "Do you know the two Arka sheaths?"—[he was indeed speaking of...]
He said to him, "Do you know the two nostrils of the Arka?"—"They are the two lips," he replied. He said to him, "Do you know the Arka-pods?"—"They are the teeth," he replied.
He said to him, "Do you know the Arka-stone?"—"It is the tongue," he replied. He said to him, "Do you know the root of the Arka?"—"It is food," he replied. This man is that Agni-Arka; whoever...

He who meditates upon this Agni-Arka Puruṣa with the knowledge, "I am this Agni-Arka," for him indeed this Agni-Arka becomes built up within his own self through that very knowledge. Verily, he who blows here is the Yajus, for as he moves, he generates all this; one should meditate upon him...
That which is produced following this [wind] is therefore the *yajus* itself.
This very space (*ākāśa*) is the *jūḥ*; for it is following this space that one speeds through the intermediate region (*antarikṣa*).
Thus, this *yajus* consists of the wind and the intermediate region, as well as that which is the *jūḥ*. Therefore, this very [wind] is the *yajus*, for it goes forth (*eti*).
This very *yajus* is established upon the *ṛc* and the *sāman*; the *ṛc* and the *sāman* carry it.

Therefore, the *adhvaryu* performs the ritual with identical cups, while the *stotra*s and *śastra*s are different from one another; it is just as if one were to cause [a horse] to gallop by means of two front legs and run by means of two hind legs—such is that. 10.3.5. [3]

Agni alone is the *puras*. For having placed Agni at the front, these creatures worship him. Āditya alone is the *caraṇa*; for when he rises, then everything here moves. This is that *yajus* together with its *puraścaraṇa* with respect to the deities (10.3.5).
Now, with respect to the self (*adhyātma*): Prāṇa alone is the *yajus*, for it is Prāṇa that, moving, generates all this. Prāṇa...
That which is born after this [breath], therefore the breath alone is the *yajus*.

10.3.5.[5] This very space is the *jūḥ*—this space that is within the self—for it is after this space that one speeds; thus this *yajus* consists of both the breath and the space, and that which is the *jūḥ*.
Therefore it is the *yajus*, for the breath indeed goes (*eti*). 10.3.5.[6]
Food indeed is the *yajus*, for by food one is born and by food one moves; this *yajus* is established in food, and it carries food.

Therefore, within the very same vital breath (*prāṇa*), various kinds of food are placed. 10.3.5. [7] Mind indeed is the *puras*; for mind is the first of the vital breaths. Sight indeed is the *caraṇa*; for by sight—

For this very Self moves; that is this *yajus*, established both with respect to the deities (*adhidevatam*) and with respect to the self (*adhyātmam*), together with its preparatory practice (*sapuraścaraṇam*).
He who knows this *yajus* thus, established both with respect to the deities and with respect to the self, together with its preparatory practice—10.3.5 [8].

He indeed becomes unharmed and uninjured, and reaches the successful conclusion of the sacrifice in safety; he becomes the best among his own people, their leader, an eater of food, and a sovereign—provided he knows this.
And as for anyone among his own people who seeks to be a rival to one who knows this, he is not at all capable of supporting his dependents. 10.3.5 [9]
Whoever experiences this, or whoever desires to support his dependents by following it, he indeed becomes capable of supporting his dependents.
This is the eldest Brahman, for there is nothing whatsoever superior to it; indeed, the eldest is the most excellent.

This belongs to his own people, for he who knows thus. 10.3.5.[11] This very Brahman is without before and without after. He who knows this Brahman as being without before and without after—among those who vie with him, no one at all becomes superior to him; rather, those who are superior to him become even more superior than he, as do other men.
From him all things are born; therefore, one should worship him as "the quarters" and "the eastern [directions]. Thus, he does not harm him. 10.3.5.

[12] Indeed, the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) of this very *yajus* is its essence. Therefore, however much of the *yajus* the Adhvaryu priest takes up for a cup-offering, that [essence] pervades both the *stotra* and the *śastra*; it extends throughout both the *stotra* and the *śastra*.

Therefore, just as the essence of food, however small it may be, sustains all food and pervades all food, so too is satisfaction his goal. Hence, when one is satisfied with food, one feels as if one has reached [one's goal]. Bliss indeed is his consciousness; bliss is his self. All the gods have bliss as their self. This, indeed, is the direct knowledge of the gods. He who knows this... (10.3.5) [13]
"He who is such as this is no mere man; he is indeed one of the gods.

(10.3.5) Knowing this, Priyavrata Rauhiṇāyana used to say: "Whether the wind blows or whether it is withheld from you, bliss is your Self. And so it blew for him exactly as it did for others. Therefore, whichever—
If one desires a blessing from among the gods, he should worship with this very [formula]: "Bliss is your self; that desire of mine—may it be fulfilled for me!
Whatever desire he may have, that desire is indeed fulfilled for him.
He who knows this attains this satisfaction, this goal, this bliss, and this Self. 10.3.5. [15]
This *yajus* is whispered and unexpressed; for the *yajus* is indeed breath (*prāṇa*), and breath has the whispered as its abode.
If someone were to say to one who expresses it clearly, "He has expressed a deity that is not to be expressed; breath shall depart from him," so indeed would it happen.
(10.3.5) But he who knows its expressed manifestation becomes manifest through fame and glory, even though [the *yajus* itself remains] whispered.

With a *yajuṣ* formula the Adhvaryu draws the cup; once drawn, it becomes manifest. With a *yajuṣ* formula he piles the fire-altar; once piled and fully constructed, it becomes manifest. With a *yajuṣ* formula he pours out the oblation; once cooked and prepared, it becomes manifest. Thus, whatever he performs silently (*upāṃśu*), once it is done and completed, it becomes manifest. This is its nature.

He who knows this manifestation as thus explained becomes manifest through renown, fame, and the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*); he quickly attains what is not yet attained, and he indeed becomes the *Yajus* itself; they call him by means of the *Yajus*.
When the gods restored Prajāpati after he had fallen apart, they placed that seed in the womb of the fire-pan (*ukhā*).
The cauldron was heated until it was as if it were a pit; for him they prepared this food within the year.
That which is this piled fire-altar, they enclosed it with his own self; being enclosed by his own self, it became his very self.
Therefore, food, when enclosed by one's own self, becomes one's very self. 10.4.1 [2]

In the same way, the sacrificer pours himself as seed into the fire-pan (ukhā) as a womb; for the fire-pan is indeed a womb. For him, he prepares this food during the year—that which is this piled fire-altar—and he encloses it within his own self.
What is enclosed within his own self becomes his very self. Therefore, food that is enclosed within one's own self becomes one's very self. 10.4.1 [3]
He places it down with the words "vauṣaṭ," for "vau" is this [earth], and "ṣaṭ" is these six layers; having thus prepared this food consisting of six layers, he covers it for him.
Food that is commensurate with one's own self protects and does not harm; that which is more than that harms, and that which is less than that does not protect. 10.4.1. [4]

This very one is the *arka*; this Agni whom they bring here is it. His food is the *arkya*; that which is this piled-up fire-altar is the *arkya* from the perspective of the *Yajus*. This very one is the *mahān* (the Great); his food is the *vratam*; that is the *Mahāvrata* from the perspective of the *Sāman*. This very one is the *ukta* (the Uttered); his food is the *thaṃ*; that is the *Uktha* from the perspective of the *Ṛc*. Thus, all this is one.
It is explained in three ways: 10.4.1.

[5] Now, Indra and Agni were created—the priesthood (*brahman*) and the nobility (*kṣatra*). Agni was indeed the priesthood, and Indra was the nobility. Once created, they remained separate; they said, "Being thus, we shall not be able to produce offspring."

"May both of you become one form in order to produce one form. Thus, those two became one form. Those two who are Indra and Agni are these two: the gold plate and the man. The gold plate is indeed Indra; the man is Agni. They are made of gold, for gold is light, and Indra and Agni are light. They are immortal.
"O Indra and Agni, [bestow] golden immortality.
(10.4.1.7) It is indeed these two, Indra and Agni, who build; for whatever consists of bricks is Agni alone. Therefore, they bake that with fire;
for whatever they bake with fire is Agni alone. Now, as for the loose soil (*purīṣa*), that is...
Therefore, they do not cook that [offering] with fire, lest it be Agni himself and not Indra. Therefore, these two, Indra and Agni, are indeed the two layers.
Now, the fire which is placed upon the built layer—that is one form; thus both become [the same]. Therefore, they [should be performed] by this very [means].

By means of form (*rūpa*), these creatures are procreated; this is indeed that single brick, for this entire fire-altar (*agni*) attains to it. That is the perfection of the bricks (*iṣṭakā-sampad*). This very same thing is the single syllable "vaḥ";
this entire fire-altar attains to it. That is the perfection of the syllables (*akṣara-sampad*). 10.4.1 [9]

Seeing this, a seer proclaimed: "I praise what has been and what is to be—the Great Brahman, the one imperishable; the manifold Brahman, the one imperishable. For indeed, into this very syllable all the gods and all beings merge. This is both the priesthood (brahman) and the nobility (kṣatra), and it is Agni alone.
Brahman is Indra; the Kṣatra is Indra and Agni; the Viś is the All-gods. The All-gods are this very thing: Brahman, Kṣatra, and Viś. 10.4.1.
[10] Knowing this, Cyāvāṛṣṇa Sāyakāyana indeed said: "Whatever work has been done for me here..."

"My subjects alone would have been completed; there would have been kings belonging to me, Brāhmaṇas belonging to me, and Vaiśyas belonging to me. But because this much of my work was completed, by that I shall behold the progeny of all [classes] in both ways.
This very one is prosperity, this is fame, this is the eater of food. 10.4.1 [11]
Cāṇḍilya, having taught this to Vāmakakṣāyaṇa, said: "You shall become prosperous, glorious, and an eater of food. Indeed, he who knows this becomes prosperous, glorious, and an eater of food.
This very Agni is Prajāpati himself. Having prepared this Agni as Prajāpati, the gods then [bestowed] upon him...
In this year, they prepared this food, which is this Mahāvratīya cup.

The Adhvaryu draws it with a cup; because he draws it, it is called a *graha*. Into it, the Udgātṛ places essence by means of the Mahāvrata. For the Mahāvrata is all these *sāmans*; thus, he places essence into it by means of all the *sāmans*.
In that [cup], the Hotṛ places essence with a great hymn (*uktha*). All these *ṛc*-verses are indeed the great hymn;
thus, he places essence in it with all the *ṛc*-verses.
When they chant the *stotra* and when he recites the *anustotra*, then, at the utterance of the *vaṣaṭ*, he offers this [libation] into him. "Vauk"—this is indeed [the sound].
Having made this food sixfold, he places it for him, measured according to his own self.
For that food which is measured according to one's own self protects and does not harm; that which is more harms, and that which is less does not protect.

This very one who has been built up as the fire-altar is indeed the *arka*; this *kyam* cup is its food, for it is the *arkya* according to the Yajus. This very one is the Great (*mahan*); this *vratam* is its food, for it is the *mahāvrata* according to the Sāman.
And this very one is the *ukta*; this *thaṃ* is its food, for it is the *uktha* according to the Ṛc. Thus, being one, it is designated in three ways. 10.4.1 [16]
This very year is Agni Prajāpati. Of him, one half consists of the Sāvitra [bricks] and the other half of the Vaiśvakarman [bricks].
Eight indeed are his parts that are Sāvitra, and eight are those that are Vaiśvakarman.
Now, whatever rite is performed between these two, that is Prajāpati himself, the seventeenfold; for he who is the part is Prajāpati.
That which is the imperishable among humans is that of the gods.

Indeed, "hair" consists of two syllables; "skin," two; "blood," two; "fat," two; "flesh," two; "sinew," two; "bone," two; and "marrow," two. These are sixteen digits (*kalā*). Now, that which moves within this interval is the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Thus Prajāpati is seventeenfold.
To this very vital breath these sixteen parts bring food. When they are unable to bring it, he consumes them and departs; therefore, when one has eaten his fill, he feels as if satisfied.

Therefore, when one is being consumed by the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), he who is thus afflicted becomes, as it were, emaciated; for he has been devoured by the vital breaths. For that seventeenfold Prajāpati, they prepared this seventeenfold food, which is this very Soma-sacrifice. Now, those sixteen parts of his are these sixteen officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); therefore, [it is not...].
"One should appoint seventeen officiating priests so that one does not exceed [the norm]. Now, whatever essence there is here, whatever oblations are offered—that indeed is the seventeenth food.
When they chant the hymns and when he recites the invitatory verses, then, at the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he offers this [oblation] into him; for this [offering] is indeed "vauk. 10.4.1. [20]
Having made this food sixfold—namely, "six"—he places it before him, measured according to his own self.
For that food which is measured according to one's own self protects and does not harm; that which is more than that harms, and that which is less than that does not protect.
This very one is the *arka* (the sun), which is this built fire-altar; its food is the *kyam*, which is this Soma sacrifice—that is the *arkya* from the perspective of the Yajus.

This very one is the *mahān* (the great); its food is the vow (*vratam*), which is the *Mahāvrata*—that is [the *mahāvrata*] from the perspective of the Sāman. This very one is the *ukta* (the spoken); its food is the *tham*, which is the *uktha*—that is [the *uktha*] from the perspective of the Ṛc. Thus, being one, it is designated in three ways. It...
Together with this food, he went upward; he who went upward is that sun, and that by which he went upward together with this food is this moon.
This very one is the *arka* (the shining one) who shines there; his food is the *kya*, and this moon is the *arkya*. This is the *arkya* from the perspective of the *Yajus*.

This very [sun] is the Great One; this is his food, his vow, thus the Mahāvrata. From the perspective of the Sāman, this very [sun] is the Uktha; this is its food, thus the Uktha. From the perspective of the Ṛc, this is that which is one, yet is declared as threefold.
Thus with respect to the deities. 10.4.1 [23]

Now, with reference to the self: the breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed the *arka*; its food is the *kya*, and that constitutes the *arkya* from the perspective of the *Yajus*. The breath is indeed the *māha*; its food is the *vrata*, and that constitutes the *Mahāvrata* from the perspective of the *Sāman*. The breath is indeed the *ukta*; its food is the *tha*, and that constitutes the *Uktha* from the perspective of the *Ṛc*. Thus, this one reality is designated in three ways; it is this very [breath].

Thus, this [Agni] consists of the deities with respect to the self (adhyātma). 10.4.2.[1] Prajāpati is indeed the year; he is Agni, King Soma, the Moon. He himself declared his own nature to Yajñavacas Rājastambāyana: "As many lights as I possess, so many bricks do I have. 10.4.2.[2]

Of this very Saṃvatsara Prajāpati, there are seven hundred and twenty days and nights as his lights; these are the *iṣṭakās*. There are three hundred and sixty *pariśrit* bricks and three hundred and sixty *yajuṣmatī* bricks.
This Saṃvatsara Prajāpati created all beings, both those that breathe and those that do not.
Having created all beings—including those without breath, both gods and humans—he felt as if he were emptied;
he was afraid of death. He reflected: "How indeed might I again gather all these beings into myself?"

Thinking again, "How indeed may I myself become the self of all these beings?", he divided himself into two parts: three hundred and sixty bricks became one part, and likewise the other part; yet he did not encompass [the whole].

He made himself threefold; there were eighty-three bricks for each part, yet he did not reach [the goal]. He made himself fourfold; there were one hundred and eighty bricks, yet he did not reach [the goal].
He made himself fivefold; there were one hundred and forty-four bricks for each part, yet he did not reach [the goal].

He made himself sixfold with one hundred and twenty bricks, but he did not pervade [the altar], nor did he become sevenfold. (10.4.2.9) He made himself eightfold with ninety bricks, but he did not pervade it. (10.4.2.10) He made himself ninefold with eighty bricks, but he did not pervade it. (10.4.2.11)

He made himself tenfold with seventy-two bricks; he did not pervade [the altar], nor did he divide into eleven parts. 10.4.2.[12] He made himself twelvefold with sixty bricks; he did not pervade [the altar], nor did he divide into thirteen parts, nor into fourteen parts. 10.4.2.[13]
He made himself fifteenfold; with forty-eight bricks he did not reach [the goal]. He made himself sixteenfold; with forty-five bricks he did not reach [the goal], nor did he become seventeenfold.

He made himself eighteenfold; there were forty bricks, but he did not encompass them, nor was he divided into nineteen parts. He made himself twentyfold; there were thirty-six bricks, but he did not encompass them, nor was he divided into twenty-one parts.
It did not become twenty-twofold nor twenty-threefold.
It made itself twenty-fourfold; it stood firm there upon thirty bricks in the fifteenth arrangement.
Because it stood firm in the fifteenth arrangement, therefore there are fifteen forms of the waxing moon.
[Regarding] the fifteen [days] of waning: 10.4.2.[18] Now, because he made himself twenty-four-fold, therefore the year consists of twenty-four half-months.
By means of these twenty-four self-forms consisting of thirty bricks each, he did not become distinct; he [remained incomplete] for fifteen days.
He saw his own forms, the *muhūrta*s, which are illuminators (*lokampṛṇā*) of the night for fifteen moments.
Because they protect for a moment (*muhūrtam*), they are called *muhūrta*s; and because, though small, they fill these worlds, they are called *lokampṛṇā*s. 10.4.2 [19]

"Verily, this [Agni] cooks all this—by means of days and nights, half-months, months, seasons, and the year; and he, in turn, cooks that which has been cooked by him. Thus said Bhāradvāja: "Agni is the cooker of the cooked, for it is by him that he cooks that which has been cooked. 10.4.2. [20]
In the course of a year, they amounted to ten thousand and eight hundred; he remained fixed there at those ten thousand and eight hundred.
Then he surveyed all beings; he beheld all beings within the threefold knowledge (the Veda) alone. 10.4.2 [21]

For this indeed is the self of all meters, of all hymns, of all vital breaths, and of all gods; this indeed exists, for that which is immortal exists, and that which is mortal is also this very thing. 10.4.2.
[22] Prajāpati reflected: "In the threefold knowledge (the Vedas) alone do all beings exist; come now, let me [place them] within the threefold knowledge itself."
"Let me fashion myself through knowledge," he thought.

He then separated the *ṛc*s; there were twelve thousand *bṛhatī*s. As many as those *ṛc*s that were created by Prajāpati stood firm in the thirty-third arrangement among the *paṅkti*s; they remained so in that thirty-third [arrangement].

They stood in an array; therefore there are thirty nights in a month. And because they were in *paṅkti* verses, Prajāpati became fivefold (*pāṅkta*). Those *paṅkti* verses amounted to eight hundred times one hundred. 10.4.2. [24] Then he separated the other two Vedas: twelve thousand *bṛhatī* verses, eight thousand of the Yajus formulas, and four thousand of the Sāmans.
Of these two Vedas, the Sāmans comprise just as much as was created by Prajāpati; they both stood upon the thirtyfold array in the Paṅktis.
Because they stood upon the thirtyfold array, there are thirty nights in a month; and because they were in the Paṅktis, Prajāpati is fivefold (pāṅkta). Those [verses] amount to exactly eight hundred.

They became verses (paṅktis). 10.4.2.[25] All those three Vedas became ten thousand and eight hundred and eighty [verses]. In every muhūrta he attained eighty [verses], and in every muhūrta eighty [verses] were completed. 10.4.2.[26]

He, having become semen, poured himself—the self consisting of the *chandas*, consisting of the *stomas*, consisting of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), and consisting of the deities—into the fire-pan as a womb within these three worlds. His first self was fashioned during the first half-month;
each subsequent one was fashioned further back, further back, until in the year itself he was fashioned entirely and completely whole. 10.4.2. [27]
In that he laid down the enclosing-stones (*pariśrit*), he laid down the night;

after that, fifteen *muhūrta*s; after each *muhūrta*, fifteen *aśītis*. And when he laid down the *yajuṣmatī* bricks, he laid down the day; after that, fifteen *muhūrta*s; after each *muhūrta*, fifteen *aśītis*. In this manner, he [laid down] these.

He deposited the triple knowledge within himself and made it his own essence. He became the very self of all beings right here—consisting of the meters, consisting of the hymns, consisting of the vital breaths, and consisting of the deities.
Having become composed of these, he ascended upwards. That which ascended is this very moon. 10.4.2 [28]
This is its foundation: he who shines yonder [the sun]. From him alone it was fashioned; upon him it was fashioned. Verily, he fashioned it from his own self;
from his own self he generated it.
When one, intending to pile the fire-altar, undergoes initiation, it is just as Prajāpati did regarding these three worlds within the fire-pan (ukhā).

Just as in the past the Self, having become semen, was poured into the womb, even so does this [sacrificer] now pour himself, having become semen, into the womb that is the fire-pan (ukhā)—consisting of the *chandas*, consisting of the *stomas*, consisting of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), and consisting of the deities. His first self is perfected in the first half-month; further back than that, another; further back than that, another. In the year itself, he becomes everything, the whole.
It is consecrated. 10.4.2.[30] In that he lays down the enclosing-stones (*pariśrit*), he thereby lays down the night; following that, fifteen *muhūrta*s;
following each *muhūrta*, fifteen *aśītis*; then, when he lays down a brick with a formula (*yajusmatī*).
On that day he deposits it; thereafter, fifteen muhūrtas; after each muhūrta, fifteen eighty-seconds (*aśīti*s).

Thus, he sows this threefold knowledge (*trayī vidyā*) into himself and makes it his own. He becomes the self of all beings here, consisting of the *candasyas*, consisting of the *stomas*, consisting of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), and consisting of the deities. Having become composed of this very [knowledge], he rises upward.

When one who knows thus departs from this world, he then attains this very Self, which consists of the *chandas*, which consists of breath (*prāṇa*), and which consists of the deities. Having become composed of these very things, he ascends upwards—whosoever, knowing thus, performs this rite, or whosoever knows this in this way. 10.4.3. [1]
The year, indeed, is death; for it is by means of days and nights that this [year] diminishes the lifespan of mortals, and then they die.

Therefore, this year is death. He who knows this year as death—for him, this [year] does not diminish his lifespan by means of days and nights before old age; he reaches his full span of life. 10.4.3. [2]
This indeed is the Ender; for by means of day and night, he reaches the end of the life-span of mortals, and then they die.
Therefore, this alone is the Ender. He who knows this year as Death does not reach the end of his life-span by day and night before old age; he indeed lives out his full span of life. 10.4.3. [3]
Those gods were afraid of this Death, the End-maker, Prajāpati, the Year, thinking, "Lest he should reach the end of our life by means of day and night.
They performed these sacrificial rites: the Agnihotra, the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the Four-Monthly sacrifices, and the Animal sacrifice.
Performing this gentle sacrifice with these sacrificial rites, they attained immortality.

They, moreover, piled the fire-altar; they laid down an unlimited number of enclosing stones (*pariśrit*), an unlimited number of *yajuṣmatī* bricks, and an unlimited number of *lokampṛṇā* bricks, just as even now some people lay them down here. Thus [it was done by] the gods.
"Because you did not do so," they indeed did not attain immortality. 10.4.3.

[6] They moved about worshipping and toiling, desiring to win immortality. Prajāpati said to them: "Verily, you do not lay down all my forms; either you leave something out or you do not complete it. Therefore, you are not immortal."
"Be [my priests]," he said. They replied, "Tell us that yourself, so that we may lay down all your forms.
He said, "Lay down three hundred and sixty enclosing-stones (pariśrit), and three hundred and sixty [other bricks]."

"Place thirty-six *yajuṣmatī* bricks, then ten thousand and eight hundred *lokampṛṇā* bricks; then you shall place all my forms upon me, and then you shall become immortal. The gods did so, and then the gods became immortal. 10.4.3 [9]

Death said to the gods, "In this very way all humans will become immortal; what, then, will be my share? They replied, "No one else besides him shall become immortal with his body; only when you take this share away, then, having turned back..."

"By means of the body one becomes immortal now; by means of knowledge or by means of ritual action one becomes immortal. As for what they said—"by means of knowledge or by means of ritual action"—this fire is indeed that knowledge, and this fire is indeed that ritual action. Those who know this thus, or those who perform this ritual action, are born again after death.

Those who come into being indeed attain immortality; but those who do not know this, or who do not perform this rite, are born again after death and become the food of that very one again and again. When he piles the fire-altar, he thereby attains this very Agni, the end-maker, Death, the Year, Prajāpati.
That which the gods attained, he places here; just as the gods then placed it, so does he. By means of the *pariśrit* bricks, he attains for him the nights;
by means of the *yajuṣmatī* bricks, the days, the half-months, the months, the seasons, the worlds, and the *ṛṇā* bricks, the muhūrtas.
Those enclosing stones (*pariṣritaḥ*) which are the worlds of the nights constitute the attainment of the nights; they are a reflection of the nights.

They number sixty and three hundred. Indeed, there are sixty and three hundred nights in a year. Of these, he encloses twenty-one around the *gārhapatya* fire, seventy-eight in the *dhiṣṇya* hearths, and two [remain].
In the one hundred and sixty-first [chapter], regarding the Āhavanīya fire (10.4.3.14): now,
the sacrificial bricks (yajuṣmatya iṣṭakāḥ) are the bunch of Darbha grass, the clod-bricks (logeṣṭakāḥ), the lotus leaf, the gold plate and the golden man, the two offering-ladles (srucau),

the naturally perforated brick (svayamātṛṇā), the Dūrvā-brick, the two bricks with two formulas (dviyajū), the two Retahsic bricks, the Viśvajyotis, the two Ṛtavyā bricks, the Aṣāḍhā brick, and the tortoise.

The mortar and pestle, the fire-pan, the five heads of animals, fifteen bricks pertaining to the waters (*apasyā*), and five meters (*candasyā*). 10.4.3.[15] Now for the second layer: five bricks pertaining to the horses (*aśvinī*), two seasonal (*ṛtavyā*) bricks, five pertaining to the Viśvedevas (*vaiśvadevī*), five breath-supporting (*prāṇabhṛt*) bricks, five pertaining to the waters, and nineteen age-matching (*vayasī*) bricks; these make forty-one, which is the second layer. 10.4.3.[16]
Now, the third layer consists of one *svayamātṛṇā* brick; five *diśyā* bricks; four *viśvajyotis* bricks; four *ṛtavyā* bricks; ten *prāṇabhṛt* bricks;
thirty-six *candasyā* bricks; and fourteen *vālakhilyā* bricks. These total seventy-one bricks for the third layer.
Now, the fourth layer consists of eighteen bricks in the first section, then twelve, and then seventeen. These [total forty-seven].
The forty-seventh is the fourth layer. 10.4.3.[18] Now the fifth [layer]: five *asapatnā* bricks; forty *virāj* bricks; twenty-nine *stomabhāga* bricks;
five *nākasad* bricks; five *pañcacūḍā* bricks; thirty-one *candasyā* bricks; eight *gārhapatya* bricks; and eight [more].

Furthermore, in the *cita* there are the two *ṛtavyā*s, the *viśvajyotis*, the *vikarṇī*, the *svayamātṛṇā*, and the speckled stone (*pṛśni-aśman*); when the fire is deposited upon the *cita*, these constitute one hundred and thirty-eight bricks, which is the fifth layer (*citi*).

The attainment of the days is thus accomplished; they are the counterpart of the days, amounting to three hundred and sixty.
For there are indeed three hundred and sixty days in a year. Now, as for the thirty-six [bricks], the *puruṣa* (filling soil) is the thirty-sixth among them;
from that, the twenty-four which are the worlds of the half-months constitute the attainment of the half-months themselves.

Now, those twelve bricks which are the worlds of the months are made the attainment of the months themselves; they are the image of the months. Those two by two bricks which are the worlds of the seasons are for the sake of the non-emptiness of the seasons. Then, those *lokampṛṇā* bricks which are the worlds of the muhūrtas are made the attainment of the muhūrtas themselves; they are the image of the muhūrtas.
There are ten thousand and eight hundred of these bricks, for there are exactly so many muhūrtas in a year. Of these, he places twenty-one on the Gārhapatya fire-altar;
eighty-two on the Dhiṣṇya hearths; and the others on the Āhavanīya. These indeed are the forms of the year; they are obtained and placed here by him.

10.4.3.[21] Regarding this, some desire to complete this total number in the Āhavanīya fire itself, saying, "These fires have been piled elsewhere; why should we look for their completion here when they have already been established? One should not do so. For he piles these ten fires—eight [in the body],...

The *dhiṣṇya* hearths, the *āhavanīya*, and the *gārhapatya*—therefore they say, "Agni is the *virāj*," for the *virāj* consists of ten syllables. Yet they designate all of them as one, namely "Agni," for these are indeed all the forms of him.
Just as the days and nights, the half-months, the months, and the seasons are the forms of the year, so too are these all the forms of him. 10.4.3 [22]

Those who act in that manner indeed place these forms of his outside; moreover, they create a state of inverted order, making the common people (viś) an adversary and a challenger to the ruling power (kṣatra). On the Āgnīdhra hearth, he places a speckled stone and then gazes upon it; why then does he gaze upon it, but not upon the others?
By means of that very [verse] with which he beholds Nirṛti, he drives away evil; that is the eleventh.
Regarding this they say: "Why does he not behold those [bricks] here? For he does not offer an oblation upon them; indeed, it is by the oblation that every brick becomes complete.

Regarding this they say: "How is it that these [bricks] are laid down so as not to exceed him? Indeed, these are his vigor; for vigor does not exceed a man. He who, knowing this, performs this rite, or he who knows this very thing, truly constructs this Prajāpati in his entirety and completeness. 10.4.4.1.
While Prajāpati was creating living beings, evil death overcame him from all sides. He performed austerity for a thousand years, desiring to cast off evil.
As he was performing that austerity, lights rose upward from these hair-pits; those which are these...
These luminaries are those very stars; as many as these stars are, so many are the hair-pores;
as many as the hair-pores are, so many are the muhūrtas of the thousand-year cycle.
In that thousandth year, he flowed out entirely; he who flowed out is this very wind which blows here.

Then he purifies; he purifies away that evil. This is the body. What man indeed could sustain it for a thousand years? Verily, by knowledge, one who knows thus sustains a thousand years. One should meditate upon all these bricks as belonging to a thousand: each enclosing-stone (*pariśrit*) with a thousand nights, and each enclosing-stone with a thousand nights.
One should worship the perfected [year] by means of a thousand days for each day-part,
by means of a thousand half-months for each half-month-part, by means of a thousand months for each month-part,
and by means of a thousand seasons for each season-part.
Every thousandth muhūrta they offer one muhūrta-portion; every thousandth year they offer one year-portion.
Those who know this Agni as thus perfected through the year—they know his thousandth part. But those who do not know him thus—they do not know even his thousandth part.

Vidura said: "He who knows this, or who performs this rite, indeed attains this entire, complete Agni Prajāpati, whom Prajāpati attained. Therefore, one who knows this should perform austerity. Whatever austerity one who knows this performs up to sexual intercourse—all that of his becomes the heavenly world. (10.4.4)

This has been declared by a Ṛgvedic verse: "The toil of those whom the gods protect is not in vain. Indeed, for one who knows this, no toil whatsoever becomes in vain; thus do the gods protect all of this for him.
Now, as for the instructions regarding the Upaniṣads: the followers of Śākāyanya worship [the fire-altar] as Vāyu and Agni; some, however, worship it as Āditya and Agni.
Now, Śraumatya or Hāliṅgava used to say:
"Vāyu indeed is Agni; therefore, whenever the Adhvaryu performs the final rite, he then enters into him alone.
Śāṭyāyani used to say: "The year indeed is Agni; of it, spring is the head, summer is the right wing," and so forth.

The rainy season is its back; the autumn season is its middle body; the winter and dewy seasons are its tail and foundation; speech is Agni; breath is Vāyu; sight is Āditya; mind is Candramas; hearing is the quarters; water is the pair;
austerity is the foundation; the months are the joints; the half-months are the veins; days and nights are the silver and golden wings; he is thus.

"He goes even to the gods"—one should indeed know that "Agni is the year," for he becomes composed of that; but one should rather know it thus: [10.4.5] Celaka Śāṇḍilyāyana used to say, "These very worlds are the three layers containing the *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks;
the sacrificer is the fourth; all desires are the fifth. By this, they perfect both these worlds and the self."

"One should know that it includes all desires," [so it is said]. Now, speech is indeed the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) of this very fire-altar; for by speech it is built—with the *ṛc*, the *yajus*, and the *sāman*. This refers to divine speech;
but as for human speech, when one says, "Do this! or "Do that!", it is by means of that [human speech] as well that it is built.
This very speech is threefold: the *ṛc*s, the *yajus* formulas, and the *sāmans*. Therefore, Agni is threefold, for he is built up by means of this triad.
And so too is this [altar] threefold; indeed, it is also threefold in this way, in that bricks of three kinds are laid upon it:
those with masculine names, those with feminine names, and those with neuter names—thus it is threefold.
Thus, these limbs of a person have masculine names, feminine names, and neuter names.

This very self (ātman) is indeed divided threefold; by means of this self divided threefold, he attains that divine, immortal state which is likewise divided threefold. All those [bricks] are called simply "bricks" (iṣṭakāḥ), and not "made of bricks" (naiṣṭaka) or "belonging to bricks" (naiṣṭakam). Such is the speech.
By means of form, speech indeed encompasses all this—whether it be female, male, or neuter—for by speech alone all this is attained.

Therefore, he settles them all with the formula, "Sit thou firm like Aṅgiras," and not with "Sit thou firm like Aṅgiras" nor "Sit thou firm like Aṅgiras"; for he thus consecrates speech itself. 10.5.1 [4]
That speech is yonder sun; he is Death. Therefore, whatever is on this side of the sun, all that is seized by Death.
If anyone builds a fire-altar on this side of it, he builds it as something already seized by Death;

By means of this knowledge, he indeed conquers repeated death; for from this point upward, this [altar] of his becomes built up.
