That which is the world of the Ṛg-verses is this;
and that which shines as this flame is the Mahāvrata, those are the Sāmans, and that is the world of the Sāmans.
And that person who is in this orb is Agni, those are the Yajus formulas, and that is the world of the Yajus formulas. 10.5.2 [7]
This very same triple science shines forth; even those who do not know this say, "This triple science indeed shines forth.
Verily, it is Speech that speaks while seeing it. This person in that orb, and this immortal radiance which shines, from that [radiance], death does not come.
For within the immortal one dies; therefore it is not seen, for within the immortal there is death.
Regarding this, there is this verse: "Within death is the immortal"—for this immortal is indeed within death;
"the immortal is placed within death"—for upon this person this orb is established and shines.

"Death clothes Vivasvat"—Vivasvat is indeed this Āditya, for he has clothed himself in day and night; him Death clothes, for he is surrounded on all sides by him. "The self of Death is Vivasvat"—for in this orb is the self of this Person. Regarding this, there is this verse: 10.5.2. [10]
Of these two—the radiance and this person—this orb is the foundation.

Therefore, one should not recite the Great Hymn (*mahaduktha*) for another, lest he destroy this foundation. He indeed destroys this foundation who recites the Great Hymn for another. Therefore, the reciter of the hymn is most abundant [in merit].
"They speak of it as 'the one who has found a firm foundation,' for he indeed becomes firmly established. This is with respect to the deities (adhidevatam).

Now, with respect to the sacrifice (adhiyajñam): That orb which shines there is this golden disk (rukma); and that brilliance which blazes is this lotus leaf (*puṣkaraparṇa*), for these waters are indeed the lotus leaf. And he who is in this orb...

This very person is that golden person; having prepared this very triad, he places it here. Following the completion of the sacrifice, he ascends upwards and enters into him who shines yonder. Therefore, one need not trouble oneself to extinguish the fire, for at that time he becomes that very thing up there. Thus it is said.
Thus with respect to the sacrifice.
Now with respect to the self (*adhyātma*): that which is this orb which shines, and this golden disk (*rukma*)—this is the white eye;
and that which is this blazing radiance, and this lotus leaf (*puṣkaraparṇa*)—this is the black eye; and that which is this...
The person who is in this maṇḍala, and this golden person—this is indeed that person who is in the right eye.
This very one is the *lokampṛṇā*; into her this entire fire (*agni*) enters completely. His mate is this [person] who is here...

In the left eye is the person; this which is the pair is indeed half of one's self. For when one is with a mate, then one is whole and complete; it is for the sake of completeness that there are two [bricks].
Since a pair is a productive couple, therefore two *lokampṛṇā* bricks are laid down at each stage; therefore, a layer is built with two [bricks].

They lead [the horse] forward. 10.5.2.[14] This very one is Indra, who is the person in the right eye; and this [other person] is Indrāṇī. For these two, the gods made this partition, the nose; therefore, one should not eat in the presence of his wife, for a vigorous son is born from him.
She brings forth one who is truly vigorous for him whose food she does not eat at the end.
This very *devavrata* (divine vow) the kinsmen of the royalty guard most closely among men;
therefore, a vigorous son is born among them. She is the "Immortal-Speaker" (*amṛtavākā*) among birds; she brings forth the swift falcon.
Having returned to the space within the heart, those two become a couple;

when they reach the end of their coupling, then this person sleeps. Just as, having reached the end of human coupling, one becomes as if unconscious, even so does he become as if unconscious at that time, for this is divine coupling.
For this, Ānanda, is the supreme bliss.
Therefore, one who knows this should sleep; for he thus causes these two deities to prosper through their beloved union.
For this reason, one should not wake a sleeping person with a sudden start, lest one disturb these two deities.
"May we become a pair and not be separated," he thinks; therefore, the mouth of one who has slept well becomes as if coated with phlegm.
It is these two deities that then pour forth seed; from that seed all this comes into being, whatever exists here.
This very one is Death: the person who is in this orb [of the sun] and the person who is here in the right eye. His feet are fixed within his heart; having pulled them out, he departs.
When he departs, then the person dies; therefore they say of one who has passed away, "His feet have been pulled out. 10.5.2. [19]

This, indeed, is the vital breath (*prāṇa*); for he leads forth all these creatures. These vital breaths are his own; when he sleeps, these vital breaths go back into him as his own (*svāpyaya*). Therefore, it is called *svāpyaya*. They cryptically call it "sleep" (*svapna*), for the gods love the cryptic. 10.5.2 [20]

When he is asleep by means of these, he knows nothing of anyone; he does not form intentions with the mind, nor does he perceive the taste of food with speech, nor does he perceive smell with the breath, nor does he see with the eye, nor does he hear with the ear; for at that time these [senses] have been merged into him. Being one, he has entered manifoldly among living beings; therefore, though she is one, she is called "the many."

The *lokampṛṇā* (space-filler) pervades the entire fire-altar; and because it is one, therefore it is single. Regarding this they say: "Is death one or many? One should reply: "It is both one and many. Insofar as it is that [Death] over there, it is one; but insofar as it is here, entered manifoldly among living beings, it is many.

Regarding this they say: "Death is near; death is far away. One should say: "It is both near and far. It is near because of that which is here within the self (*adhyātma*); it is far because of that which is there beyond. On this point there is this verse: "Resting upon food, he shines, the immortal one in the flowing together of essences."* *Chāndogya Upaniṣad 10.5.2.23*
"That which shines as this orb is food; and he who is the person within this orb is the eater.
He shines resting upon that food"—this is with respect to the deities (adhidevatam).
Now, with respect to the self (adhyātmam): this very body is food; and he who is the person in the right eye is the eater. He...
It shines resting upon this food. 10.5.2.
[25] Regarding this very [Self], the Adhvaryus worship it as Agni, for he joins together all this;
the Chandogas worship it as Sāman, for all this is unified in him; the Bahvṛcas worship it as Uktha, for he is this...

"It raises everything; therefore, those who know the *yātu* call it *yātu*. It is the 'poison' (*viṣa*), so say the serpents. It is 'serpent' (*sarpa*), so say those who know the serpent. It is 'vital energy' (*ūrj*), so say the gods. It is 'wealth' (*rayi*), so say human beings. It is 'illusion' (*māyā*), so say the Asuras. It is 'self-offering' (*svadhā*), so say the ancestors. It is 'divine folk' (*devajana*), so say those who know the divine folk. It is 'form' (*rūpa*), so say the Gandharvas. It is 'fragrance' (*gandha*), so say the Apsarases. Whatever [aspect] one meditates upon, that very thing [one becomes]."
It becomes that; having become that, it protects them. Therefore, one who knows this should worship him with all these [forms].
For all this becomes that, and having become all this, it protects him.
This Agni consists of three bricks: the *Ṛc* is one, the *Yajus* is one, and the *Sāman* is one. Now, whatever *Ṛc* he places here, it is the gold plate (*rukma*).
Thus, that which is [recited] with the *ṛc* has the person as its abode; and that which is [recited] with the *yajus* has the person as its abode;
and that which is [recited] with the *sāman* has the lotus-leaf as its abode. Thus, it consists of three bricks. These two—the gold plate (*rukma*) and the lotus-leaf—both merge into this person.
The Ṛgveda is its head, the Yajurveda its mouth, and the Sāmaveda its belly; thus it consists of one brick.
This very person who is in that orb [of the sun], and this person who is in the right eye—he becomes the self of one who knows thus. He is indeed death. 10.5.2. [28]
When one who knows this departs from this world, he then attains this very Self; he becomes immortal, for Death becomes his Self. 10.5.3.
[1] Verily, in the beginning, this was neither non-existent nor existent. There was, as it were, something here in the beginning, yet it was not. That was Mind.
Thus it was.
Therefore, this has been declared by the Seer: "At that time, there was neither non-existence nor existence. For the mind was neither existent nor non-existent.
This very mind, once created, desired to become manifest—more defined, more substantial.

Then he sought after himself; he performed that austerity. It coalesced, and it beheld thirty-six thousand fires of its own self—fires that were Arka-fires, consisting of mind, built of mind. They were established by the mind alone, they were piled by the mind alone; by the mind the cups were drawn for them, by the mind they chanted, by the mind they recited, and whatever else there was.

Whatever sacrificial rite is performed at a sacrifice—whatever rite is worthy of sacrifice—it was performed as consisting of mind, among those [fires] which consist of mind and are conscious of mind. Whatever these beings here conceive with their minds, that is indeed their performance; they lay them down, they pile them up; in them they draw the cups, in them they chant hymns, in them they recite.
They praise this: such indeed is the majesty of the mind, such its creation, and such is the extent of the mind.
There are thirty-six thousand fires that are suns; each one of them is as great as that former one.
That mind created speech. This speech, once created, desired to become manifest—more defined, more substantial.

She sought after her own self; she practiced austerity; she fainted away; she beheld thirty-six thousand fires of her own self, which were *arks* consisting of speech, built of speech. By speech alone they were maintained; by speech the cups were drawn for them; they chanted with speech; they recited with speech—whatever ritual act is performed in the sacrifice, whatever [it may be].

The sacrificial rite was performed by speech alone among those things consisting of speech, among those things known through speech, and among those things made of speech. Whatever these beings here speak with speech, that is their very work;
they establish them, they pile them up, they draw the cups for them, they chant praises for them, and they recite hymns for them. Such indeed is the manifestation of speech, such is its extent.
The emission was of this extent: thirty-six thousand fires, each one of which was as large as that former one.
That Speech emitted Breath. This Breath, once emitted, desired to become manifest—more defined, more substantial. It...

He sought the Self; he practiced austerity; he concentrated himself; he beheld thirty-six thousand fires of his own self, which were Arka-fires consisting of breath (*prāṇa*), built of breath. They were established by breath alone, they were piled up by breath alone; by breath the cups were drawn for them, by breath they chanted, and by breath they recited whatever [else there was].

Whatever sacrificial rite is performed in a sacrifice—whatever rite is worthy of sacrifice—it is performed within those made of breath, those consisting of breath, those whose consciousness is breath; it was performed as something made of breath. And whatever these beings breathe with breath, that is their very work:
they establish them, they pile them up, they draw the cups for them, they chant praises for them, they perform rituals for them.

They praise this: "Such indeed is the majesty of breath, such is its creation, such is breath. [10.5.3.6] That breath created sight. This sight, once created, desired to become manifest—more defined, more substantial. It sought after itself; it practiced austerity; it coalesced, and it became thirty-sixfold.
He saw thousands of his own fires, which were suns consisting of sight, piled with sight; they were laid out by sight alone,
they were built up by sight alone, by sight the cups were drawn for them,
they chanted with sight, and they recited with sight— whatever ritual act is performed at the sacrifice, whatever sacrificial act there is, it was done by sight alone.

In those [bricks] consisting of that eye, which are themselves consciousnesses of the eye, the eye was made to consist of the eye. Whatever these beings here see with the eye, that is the work of those very [bricks]; they place them down, they pile them up;
in them they draw the cups, in them they chant praises, in them they recite hymns. Such indeed is the manifestation of the eye, such its creation, and such is the extent of the eye.

36.10.5.3 [7] That Eye created that Ear. Once created, this Ear desired to become manifest, more defined, and more substantial; it sought after its own self, it practiced austerity, and it coalesced into thirty-six [parts].
He saw thousands of his own fires, which were the suns consisting of hearing, built by hearing; they were studied by hearing alone,
they were piled up by hearing alone, the cups were drawn for them by hearing alone, they chanted with hearing alone, and they recited with hearing alone—
whatever ritual act is performed at a sacrifice, whatever sacrificial rite there is, it was all performed by hearing alone upon those fires consisting of hearing.
In the consciousness of the ear, the ear was fashioned. Whatever these beings here hear with the ear—that is their very creation;

it is upon them that it bestows [the sacrifice], they who pile it up, in whom they draw the cups, in whom they chant the praises, and in whom they recite the hymns. Such indeed is the manifestation of the ear, such is its emanation; so great is the ear. Thirty-six [verses]. 10.5.3. [8]
From that, he created action (*karman*); it coagulated toward the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), becoming this mass, a mass of food.
Indeed, action is incomplete without the vital breaths, and the vital breaths are indeed incomplete without action. 10.5.3 [9]
This very action, once created, desired to become manifest—more defined, more embodied.

It sought after its own self; it practiced austerity. It coalesced, and it beheld thirty-six thousand fires of its own self, which were suns consisting of action, built of action, and established by action alone.
By means of action they were accumulated; by means of action the cups were drawn for them; they praised with action; they recited with action.

Whatever ritual act is performed at a sacrifice, whatever sacrificial act there is—all that was performed as consisting of action, as made of action, and as rooted in action, within those who were themselves made of action. And whatever action these beings here perform, it belongs to them alone.

That creative act (kṛti) establishes those very things; they pile them up; in them they draw the cups (graha); in them they chant the hymns (stotra); in them they recite the liturgical formulas (śastra). Such indeed is the expansion of action, such is its manifestation, such is action. Thirty-six [is that number]. That action created Agni; Agni is indeed the more manifest form of action, for by means of action they produce him.
By means of action they kindle him.
This Agni, once created, desired to become manifest—more defined, more embodied. He sought after himself; he practiced austerity; he coalesced; he [became] thirty-six...

He saw thousands of fires of his own, consisting of fire, piled with fire; they were studied by means of fire, piled by means of fire, and the cups were drawn for them by means of fire. They praised with fire, they recited with fire; whatever ritual act is performed at the sacrifice, whatever sacrificial rite there is—all that was performed by means of fire alone upon those fires consisting of fire, piled with fire, which themselves consisted of fire.

Now, whatever these beings kindle as fire—that is their own work; they establish those very fires, they pile them up, they draw cups for them, they chant praises for them, and they recite hymns for them. Such indeed is the manifestation of Agni, such is his creation, and such is Agni: thirty-six thousand sun-like fires, each one of which is as great as that [sun].

[10.5.3] These [fires] are indeed built of knowledge alone; for one who knows this, all beings build them at all times, even while he sleeps. By means of knowledge alone, these [fires] become built for one who knows this. [10.5.4] These [fires] are indeed built of knowledge alone; for one who knows this, all beings build them at all times, even while he sleeps.
By means of knowledge alone, these [fires] become built for one who knows this.

This world indeed is this built-up fire-altar. Of it, the waters are the enclosing stones; human beings are the *yajuṣmatī* bricks; the *sūdadohas* verses are the plants and trees; the loose earth is the oblations; the fuel-sticks are the fire; and the *lokampṛṇā* brick is the fire itself. All this, indeed, becomes the fire-altar; the entire fire-altar becomes the *lokampṛṇā* brick. That...
He who knows this thus—this whole world, having come into being, attains him as the *lokampṛṇā* (space-filler). 10.5.4.

[2] But indeed, this fire-altar when piled is the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). Of it, the *pariśrit* bricks are the very junction of heaven and earth; for beyond the intermediate space, heaven and earth are joined together. Those *pariśrit* bricks are birds; the *yajuṣmatī* bricks are the rain.

The *sūdadohas* verses are the rays; the excrement is the oblations; the fuel-sticks are the wind; the *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks are the sky. All this, indeed, merges into the wind alone. Thus, the entire fire-altar is piled as the sky. Of that, the waters are the enclosing stones (*pariśrit*), just as this chest is closed up.

Thus these worlds are within the waters; those waters which are beyond these worlds are the enclosing-stones (*pariśrit*). The gods are the *yajuṣmatī* bricks; whatever food there is in this world is the *sūdadohas*; the stars are the loose earth (*purīṣa*); the oblations are the fuel-sticks (*samidh*);
and the sun is the *lokampṛṇā*. All this indeed becomes the sun alone; that is the whole Agni. 10.5.4. [4]
This built-up fire-altar is indeed the sun. Its enclosing stones are the quarters;
they number three hundred and sixty, for three hundred and sixty rays of light encircle the sun on all sides from every direction.
The *yajuṣmatī* bricks are the rays; they also number three hundred and sixty, for three hundred and sixty...

There are a hundred rays of the sun; thus, when he assigns the *yajuṣmatī* bricks to the enclosing-stones, he thereby assigns the rays to the quarters. Now, that which is between the quarters and the rays is the *sūdadohas*. Furthermore, the food that is in the quarters and in the rays is the *purīṣa*; those are the oblations, those are the fuel-sticks. And as for [the words] "the quarters" and "the rays"—
And it is called the *Lokampṛṇā* (space-filler). Indeed, all this is called both "the quarters" and "the rays.
All this is Agni.
But this piled fire-altar is indeed the stars; these stars are twenty-seven, twenty-seven in number.
There are twenty-seven lunar mansions, and each one attends upon [the sun] in turn;
these amount to seven hundred and twenty, plus thirty-six. Of these, the seven hundred and twenty are indeed the bricks;
three hundred and sixty are the *pariśrit* bricks, and three hundred and sixty are the *yajuṣmatī* bricks; then there are those which are in addition.
Thirty-six is that thirteenth month; it is the self. Thirty is the self, two are the foundation, and two are the head—thus they are thirty-six.
As for why there are two [for the head], it is because the head has two syllables. Now, what is between the constellations (*nakṣatra*) is the *sūdadohas* verse;
and whatever food is in the constellations is the *purīṣa*, those are the oblations, and those are the fuel-sticks. And then...
That which is called "the constellations" (nakṣatra) is the Lokampṛṇā; indeed, all this is called "the constellations," and that is the entire Agni.
These, moreover, are twenty-one Bṛhatīs; the heavenly world is twenty-onefold, and the Bṛhatī is the heavenly world; thus, this—
He attains the heavenly world, the twenty-one-fold *stoma*, and the *bṛhatī* metre. 10.5.4.
Indeed, this piled fire-altar is the metres; these are the seven metres, each increasing by four syllables, consisting of triplets.
Of them, there are seven hundred and twenty syllables, plus thirty-six. Now, as for those seven hundred...

There are twenty *iṣṭakās*; those [additional] *pariśrit* bricks are three hundred and sixty, and the *yajuṣmatī* bricks are also three hundred and sixty. Now, as for the thirty-six that remain over, that is the thirteenth month; it is the self (*ātman*).

Thirty are the self, two are the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*), two are the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), and two are the head. As for why there are two [for the head], it is because the word "head" (*śiras*) has two syllables.
The Head (Śiras), 10.5.4 [8]:

Of this very same Bṛhatī consisting of thirty-six syllables, those which are the first ten syllables are a ten-syllable *ekapadā*; then those which are twenty are a twenty-syllable *dvipadā*; and then those which are thirty...
The Virāj consists of thirty syllables; then those which are thirty-three, that is the Trayastriṃśa consisting of thirty-three syllables;

then those which are thirty-four, that is the Catustriṃśa consisting of thirty-four syllables; and then that which is built with all the meters, this Agni, is the Atichandas. All these, indeed, are simply bricks—brick by brick.
There are three syllables; the Gāyatrī has three feet. Therefore, this Agni is of the nature of the Gāyatrī. "Earth, water"—these are three syllables; the Gāyatrī has three feet.
Thus, he is likewise of the nature of the Gāyatrī. Now, that which lies between the two metres is the Sūdadohas.
Furthermore, whatever food is in the metres, that is the *purīṣa* (filling); those are the oblations, those are the fuel-sticks. And as for that which is called "the metres," [it is so].

That is the *Lokampṛṇā*; indeed, all these are called the *Candāṃsi* (Metres). That is the whole Agni. These, indeed, are twenty-one *Bṛhatīs*. The heavenly world is twenty-onefold; the *Bṛhatī* is the heavenly world.
Thus, he attains the heavenly world, the twenty-onefold *Stoma*, and the *Bṛhatī* metre.

This built-up fire-altar is indeed the year. Its enclosing stones (*pariśrit*) are the nights; they are three hundred and sixty, for there are indeed three hundred and sixty nights in a year. The days are the *yajuṣmatī* bricks; they are also three hundred and sixty, for there are indeed three hundred and sixty days.

Now, the days of the year—those thirty-six bricks which exceed [the others]—are that thirteenth month, the self; and those half-months and months: there are twenty-four half-months and twelve months. Now, what is between day and night is the *sūdadohas*; and whatever food is in the days and nights is the *purīṣa*, those are the oblations, those are they.
Then, as for that which is called "the fuel-sticks" (*samidhaḥ*) and "days and nights" (*ahorātrāṇi*), that is the *lokapṛṇā* (space-filler).
Indeed, all this is called "days and nights"; thus, the entire fire-altar (*agni*) is filled.
These, moreover, are twenty-one *bṛhatī* verses. The heavenly world is twenty-onefold, and the *bṛhatī* is the heavenly world; thus, this [altar] is that.
He attains the heavenly world, the twenty-one-fold hymn-form (*stoma*), and the *bṛhatī* metre. 10.5.4.

[12] This piled fire-altar is indeed the self; its enclosing stones are his bones. They number three hundred and sixty, for there are indeed three hundred and sixty bones in a human being. The marrow is the *yajuṣmatī* bricks.

Those bricks amount to three hundred and sixty; for there are indeed three hundred and sixty marrow-bones in a person. Now, as for those thirty-six bricks that remain over, that is the thirteenth month, the self, the breath. Of that [year], there are thirty parts in the body, two in the foundation, and two in the head; thus, those two [in the head].

The head of yours is indeed the *dvikapāla* (two-brick) [layer]; that by which these joints are connected is the *sūdadohas*. Then, that triad by which this self (*ātman*) is covered—namely hair, skin, and flesh—that is the *purīṣa* (filling soil). What one drinks are the oblations (*āhutis*); what one eats are the fuel-sticks (*samidhas*). And that which is called "self" (*ātman*) is the *lokampṛṇā* (space-filler brick). That indeed...

All this is declared to be the Self; all that is fire. These indeed are the twenty-one *bṛhatī* verses. Indeed, all beings and all the gods are this built-up fire (*agni-cita*). Water, verily, is all the gods and all beings.

These waters are indeed this built-up fire-altar; its navigable rivers are the enclosing-stones (*pariśrit*). They number three hundred and sixty, for three hundred and sixty navigable rivers encircle the sun on all sides. The sacrificial bricks (*iṣṭakā*) accompanied by formulas (*yajuṣmatī*) are likewise navigable rivers; they also number three hundred and sixty, for three hundred and sixty...
And the hundred rivers flow toward the sun; that which is between the two navigable waters is the *sūdadohas*.
Now, those thirty-six bricks which exceed [the total] are the thirteenth month, the self; he is this very golden person. 10.5.4. [15]
These are its two foundations: the gold plate and the lotus leaf; the waters and the solar disc are the two offering-ladles;

the two arms are Indra and Agni; the two naturally-perforated bricks are this earth and the intermediate space; the three Viśvajyotis bricks are these deities—Agni, Vāyu, and Āditya—for these deities indeed are the universal light; the twelve seasonal bricks are the year, which is the self.

The five Pañcacūḍā bricks are those gods who are that sacrifice; then, as for the Vikarṇī and the Svayamātṛṇā brick, and the speckled stone which is placed upon the piled fire-altar—that is the thirty-fifth Lokampṛṇā brick. The Yajus formula is the thirty-sixth; this is his very self at the end of all. He is in the midst of all the waters; he is endowed with all desires.

Water, indeed, is all desires; yet this [Self] is desireless, possessing all desires, for no one has any desire for it. Regarding this, there is this verse: "By means of knowledge they ascend to that place where desires have vanished; neither those who give sacrificial gifts nor those who practice austerity go there. Indeed, that world is not attained by sacrificial gifts.
One who knows this eats through austerity alone; for that world belongs indeed to those who know this. 10.5.4.

[17] The cloud is the loose soil, the moon is the oblations, and the stars are the fuel. When the moon dwells in a star, then the oblation dwells in the fuel; this indeed is the food of the oblation, this its foundation. Therefore, the oblation does not perish.
This [earth] diminishes, for this is its food; this is its foundation. Now, that which is called "the gods" (*devāḥ*) is the *lokaṃpṛṇā* brick.
Indeed, all this is called "the gods.
Regarding this, it is declared in a Ṛgvedic verse: "O All-Gods (*viśve devāḥ*), after you [comes] this Yajus. For here all beings and all [deities] are present.

The gods become the *yajus* itself; thus, all this becomes the *lokampṛṇā*. He who knows this thus—having become this *lokampṛṇā*, all this becomes him. These, indeed, are twenty-one *bṛhatī*s; the heavenly world is twenty-onefold, and the *bṛhatī* is the heavenly world; thus, this...
He attains the heavenly world, the twenty-one-fold *stoma*, and the *bṛhatī* metre. 10.5.5.
Kuśri Vājaśravasa built a fire-altar. Suśruvā Kauṣya said to him, "O Gautama, since you have built this fire-altar, did you build it facing forward?"
"You have worshipped him facing toward you; you have worshipped him facing away from you; you have worshipped him facing upward.
[10.5.5.2] "If you have worshipped him facing forward, it is just as if one were to bring food from behind to someone sitting with his face turned away; such will your oblation not accept. [10.5.5.3]

"But if you laid it down facing westward, why then did you make its tail behind? (10.5.5.4) And if you laid it down facing downward, that would be as if one were to place food upon the back of someone lying face down;
in that way, your oblation will not accept it. (10.5.5.5)
"But if you have laid him out face upwards," [he said], "the bird does not carry one who is face upwards to the heavenly world;
it will not carry you to the heavenly world, and it will be non-heavenly for you.
He replied, "I have laid him facing eastward; I have laid him facing westward."
"We have piled him facing downward; we have piled him facing upward; we have piled him in all directions.

When he piles the man facing eastward and the two offering-ladles facing eastward, it is piled facing eastward. Then, when he piles the tortoise facing westward and the heads of the animals facing westward, it is piled facing westward. And as for [the one] facing downward...
He places the tortoise; the animal heads are turned downward, the bricks are turned downward—thus it is built facing downward.
Now, when he places the Puruṣa facing upward, the two offering-ladles are turned upward, the mortar is turned upward, and the fire-pan is turned upward—thus it is built facing upward.
Then, when he places the bricks crawling all around the quarters...
That [fire-altar] is piled up on all sides. Now, while they were having the coffers carried, they caused them to carry the fire-altar with its head removed.
One among them said, "The head is indeed prosperity (*śrī*). They have stripped his prosperity away; he will suffer total ruin. And so it indeed came to pass.
Then one said: "The vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are indeed the head; he has torn out his vital breaths; he will go quickly to that world.
And it was exactly so. 10.5.5.
[10] This [altar] is built upright: namely, the bunch of *darbha* grass, the clod-bricks, and the lotus leaf.

The two offering-spoons with golden men, the naturally-perforated brick, the *dūrveṣṭakā*, the two *dviryajuṣ* bricks, the two *retaḥsic* bricks, the *viśvajyotis*, the two seasonal (*ṛtavyā*) bricks, the *aṣāḍhā*, and the tortoise—now, this very thing is his most manifest head, namely the fire which is deposited upon the piled altar; therefore, one must not remove it. 10.6.1. [1]
Now, these men— Aruṇa Aupaveśi, Satyayajña Pauluṣi, Mahāśāla Jābāla,
Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi, Indradyumna Bhāllaveya, and Jana Śārkarākṣya— once came together and sat down for a discussion concerning Vaiśvānara.
However, they did not reach a consensus regarding Vaiśvānara.
They said, "This Aśvapati Kaikeya indeed knows Vaiśvānara at this time; let us go to him.

They went to Aśvapati Kaikeya, and he assigned them separate dwellings, separate honors, and separate Soma-offerings for a thousand [vessels] each. In the morning, still not having reached an agreement among themselves, they approached him with fuel in their hands.
They approached him, saying, "We have come to you.

He said, "What is this, venerable sirs, that you who are learned in the Vedas and the sons of those learned in the Vedas ask? They replied, "The venerable one knows Vaiśvānara thoroughly; tell it to us. He said, "Indeed, I know it thoroughly now."
"Having approached, he placed fuel on the Vaiśvānara fire, saying, 'You have come.
He said to Āruṇi Aupaveśi, "Gautama, as what do you know Vaiśvānara to be? "The earth alone, O King," he replied. "Yes," he said, "this indeed is Vaiśvānara; for this is the foundation."

"You know Vaiśvānara; therefore you are firmly established with offspring and cattle. Indeed, he who knows this Vaiśvānara as the foundation conquers recurrent death and attains a full lifespan. But these two are the feet of Vaiśvānara;
your feet would have withered away had you not come here. Thus it was that your feet remained unknown to you.
"If you had not come," [he said].

Then he said to Satyayajña Pauluṣi, "O Prācīnayogya, whom do you know as Vaiśvānara? "Water alone, O King," he replied. "Yes," he said, "this indeed is Vaiśvānara as wealth (rayi), for you have indeed known this wealth."

"You know Vaiśvānara; therefore, you possess wealth and prosperity. Indeed, whoever knows this Vaiśvānara as wealth conquers recurrent death and attains a full lifespan. This is the bladder of Vaiśvānara; had you not come, your bladder would have burst. Had you not come, your bladder would have remained unknown to you."
Then he said to Mahāśāla Jābāla, "Aupamanyava, whom do you know as Vaiśvānara?
"Space alone, O King," he replied. "Yes," he said, "this indeed is the abundant Vaiśvānara; for this..."

"You know Vaiśvānara extensively; therefore, you are abundant in offspring and cattle. Indeed, he who knows this Vaiśvānara extensively conquers rebirth and attains a full lifespan. This is the very self of Vaiśvānara. Your self would have perished had you not come here; for your self would have remained unknown to you."
"Or [he thought], 'He will not come.
10.6.1.[7] Then he said to Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi Vaiyāghrapadya, "O King, whom do you know as Vaiśvānara?
He replied, "Vāyu alone, O King. [The other] said, "Yes. [The first] said, "This indeed is Vaiśvānara of the manifold paths; for this..."

"You know Vaiśvānara as having separate paths; therefore, rows of chariots follow you in separate lines. Indeed, he who knows this Vaiśvānara as having separate paths conquers recurrent death and attains a full lifespan.
This is the breath of Vaiśvānara; your breath would have departed had you not come."
"Your vital breath (*prāṇa*) would have remained unknown to you had you not come," he said. Then he spoke to Indradyumna Bhāllaveya: "O Vaiyāghrapadya, whom do you know as Vaiśvānara?
"The sun alone, O King," he replied. "Yes," he said, "this indeed is Vaiśvānara of Sublime Splendor (*sutatejas*), for this one—"

"You know Vaiśvānara of well-kindled splendor; therefore, this son of yours remains in the house, being consumed and cooked yet not perishing. Indeed, he who knows this Vaiśvānara of well-kindled splendor conquers rebirth and attains a full lifespan. This eye of yours is indeed the eye of Vaiśvānara; it would have burned you had you not [known this]."

"If he had not come, your eye would have remained unknown to you—or rather, it would have been as if he had not come. Then he said to Jana Śārkarākṣya, "Sāyavasa, whom do you know as Vaiśvānara? "Only the sky, O King," he replied. "Yes," he said, "this indeed is the Vaiśvānara who stands above (Atiṣṭhā). For you have indeed known him as the one who stands above."

"You know Vaiśvānara; therefore, you stand above your equals. Verily, he who knows this Vaiśvānara as the one who transcends [all] conquers recurrent death and attains a full lifespan. This is the head of Vaiśvānara;
your head would have been struck off had you not come," or rather, "your head would have remained unknown to you had you not come. (10.6.1)
He said to them: "Indeed, you have each known Vaiśvānara separately and have eaten food separately.

The gods, however, having well understood him, attained him as one who is the size of a span. But I shall explain him to you in such a way that I will make him out to be exactly the size of a span. 10.6.1 [11]

He said, pointing to the head: "This indeed is Vaiśvānara as the Pre-eminent. Pointing to the eyes, he said: "This indeed is Vaiśvānara of Brilliant Splendor. Pointing to the nostrils, he said: "This indeed is Vaiśvānara of Diverse Paths. Pointing to the space within the mouth, he said: "This indeed is Vaiśvānara the Abundant."
Pointing to the principal waters, he said, "This is Vaiśvānara, indeed, wealth. Pointing to the chin, he said, "This is Vaiśvānara, indeed, the foundation. This very Agni Vaiśvānara is the person;
he who knows this Agni Vaiśvānara thus, as having the form of a person within the person—
One who knows this becomes firmly established; he overcomes repeated death, attains a full lifespan, and Vaiśvānara does not harm him even when he speaks.
This world is indeed twofold: the eater and the food. When these two come together, it is called "the eater," not "the food."

He who is that eater is indeed Agni; whatever they place upon him are his fuel-sticks (*āhitayaḥ*). These very things are what they call "oblations" (*āhutayaḥ*) cryptically; for the gods love the cryptic. 10.6.2 [3] Or rather, the eater is Āditya, and the moon is his fuel-sticks, for the moon is placed within Āditya.
"Placing"—this refers to the deities (adhidevatam).

Now, with respect to the self (adhyātmam): the eater is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and its offerings are the food, for the vital breath places the food; thus it is said of Agni. Now, as for Arka: Agni is indeed the Arka, and his offerings are *kam* (pleasure), for the offerings are for the pleasure of Agni.

The Sun is indeed the *arka*; its *kaṃ* is the Moon, for the Moon is indeed *kaṃ* for the Sun. This is with respect to the deities. Now, with respect to the self: the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed the *arka*; its *kaṃ* is food (*anna*), for food is indeed *kaṃ* for the vital breath.
Such is the meaning of *arka*.

Now, regarding the *uktha*: Agni is indeed the *uk*, and the oblations are the *tham*; for by means of the oblations, Agni arises. (10.6.2.9) Regarding the deities: Āditya is indeed the *uk*, and the Moon is the *tham*; for by means of the Moon, Āditya arises. This is with respect to the deities. (10.6.2.10) Now, with respect to the self (*adhyātma*): Prāṇa is indeed the *uk*, and food is the *tham*; for by means of food, Prāṇa arises. (10.6.2.11)

Verily, this Puruṣa is of the nature of the *agni*, of the nature of the *arka*, and of the nature of the *uktha*. He who worships this Puruṣa as such—as being of the nature of the *agni*, of the nature of the *arka*, and of the nature of the *uktha*—his rival truly withers away, for he knows thus. 10.6.2. [11]
By means of breath, fire blazes; by means of fire, wind; by means of wind, the sun; by means of the sun, the moon; by means of the moon, the stars;
by means of the stars, lightning. Such indeed is the radiance in this world and in that world.
He who knows this blazes with all that radiance in this world and in that world. 10.6.3.1.

"One should meditate on Brahman as Truth. Now, this person consists of volition (*kratu*); whatever his volition is when he departs from this world, with that same volition he passes into the next world and becomes [one with it]. (10.6.3) He should meditate on the Self as consisting of mind, having breath for its body, whose form is light, and whose essence is space."
Capable of assuming any form at will, swift as thought, whose resolve is truth and whose steadfastness is truth; possessing all fragrances and all tastes, abundant in every direction;
pervading this entire universe, yet remaining unspoken and indifferent—like a grain of rice, or a grain of barley, or a grain of *śyāmāka* millet.
Or like a grain of wild rice—this golden person within the inner self is like smokeless light. He is greater than heaven, greater than the ether, greater than this earth, and greater than all beings.
He is the self of breath; he is my self. "After departing from here, I shall attain that self," [he said].

"He who should have this certain knowledge has no doubt," so said Śāṇḍilya; "this is indeed so. Dawn is the head of the sacrificial horse, the sun its eye, the wind its breath, and Vaiśvānara fire its open mouth. The year is the body of the sacrificial horse; heaven is its back, the intermediate space its belly, and the earth its underbelly.
The belly is the quarters; the sides are the intermediate directions; the ribs are the seasons; the limbs are the months and half-months;
the joints are the days and nights; the foundation is the lunar mansions; the bones are the sky; the flesh is the sands;
the entrails are the rivers; the liver and the lungs are the mountains; and the herbs and trees are the undigested food.
Its forepart is the rising [sun] and its hindpart is the setting [sun]; when it yawns, that is lightning;
when it shakes itself, that is thunder; when it urinates, that is rain. Speech is its speech.
By day, the *mahiman* cup was born before the horse from the front; its source is the eastern ocean. Night [was born] behind it.
After him was born Mahiman (the Great One). His source is in the western ocean. These two, indeed, Mahiman and Aśva, were produced on both sides of the horse.
Having become a steed (*haya*), he carried the gods; as a stallion (*vājī*), the Gandharvas; as a racer (*arvan*), the Asuras; as a horse (*aśva*), human beings.
The ocean is his kinsman, the ocean is his source. 10.6.5.1.

In the beginning, there was nothing whatsoever here; this was covered by death alone, by hunger, for hunger is death. He created the mind, thinking, "May I have a self. He moved about performing *arcana* (worship/effort). As he performed *arcana*, water was produced.
"While I was performing *arcana*, what (*kam*) has come into being for me," he thought. That is the essence of the *arka*; indeed, happiness (*kam*) comes to him who knows this.
Thus, one knows the "arke" nature of the *arka*.
10.6.5.[2] Water, indeed, is the *arka*. That which was the froth of the waters solidified;
it became the earth. Upon it, he exerted himself. From him, thus exerted and heated, his essence and vital energy (*tejas*) issued forth as fire. 10.6.5.[3]
He divided himself threefold: the sun as one third and the wind as one third.

This very breath is thus established in a threefold manner. Of it, the eastern direction is the head; those two [intermediate directions] are the two arms. Then, its western direction is the tail; those two [intermediate directions] are the two thighs. The southern and northern directions are the two sides.
The sky is its back, the intermediate space its belly, and this [earth] its chest. This very one is established in the waters;
wherever it goes, there it finds support—so it is for one who knows this.
He desired, "May a second self be born to me. Through his mind, he entered into union with speech.
Death arose from hunger; that which was semen became the year. Before that, there was no year.
He bore him for as long as a year, and after that time, he brought him forth. When he was born, Death opened his mouth to devour him; he made the sound "bhāṇ," and that became speech. 10.6.5 [5]

He thought, "If I should think of this [world] as food, I shall make very little food. With that speech and with that self, he created all this—whatever exists here: the Ṛg-verses, the Yajus-formulas, the Sāman-chants, the meters, the sacrifices, progeny, and cattle. Whatever he created, he resolved to eat; therefore, it is called "All-eater" (*sarvāt*).
That is the Aditi-nature of Aditi. He who thus knows this Aditi-nature of Aditi becomes the eater of all; everything becomes his food.
10.6.5 [6] He desired, "May I sacrifice again with a greater sacrifice. He exerted himself and practiced austerity. Of him, thus exerted...
The glory and vigor of the heated [body] departed; for glory and vigor are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). When the vital breaths had departed, the body was about to swell.
His mind remained within that very body. He desired: "May this become fit for sacrifice for me; may I become embodied through it. Thereupon, he became a horse.
When it was cooked, he thought, "It has become fit for sacrifice. That is precisely why the Aśvamedha is called the Aśvamedha.
He truly knows the Aśvamedha who knows it thus.
He did not wish to confine it; at the end of a year, he sacrificed it as his own self.
He drove the animals away from the deities; they immolated that which had been sprinkled as belonging to all the deities, [saying] "it belongs to Prajāpati.
This indeed is the Aśvamedha, namely he who shines yonder; the year is his body, and this fire is the *arka*; these worlds are its...
These two selves are indeed the *arka* and the *medha*, yet they become one single deity, namely Death itself. He conquers repeated death;
death does not reach him; death becomes his self; he attains a full lifespan; he becomes one with these deities—he who knows thus. 10.6.5. [9]

Now, the lineage is the same up to the son of Sāñjīvī: the son of Sāñjīvī [received it] from Māṇḍūkāyani; Māṇḍūkāyani from Māṇḍavya; Māṇḍavya from Kautsa; Kautsa from Māhitthi; Māhitthi from Vāmakakṣāyaṇa; and Vāmakakṣāyaṇa from Vātsya.
Śāṇḍilya from Acaṇḍilya; Acaṇḍilya from Kuśri; Kuśri from Yajñavacas Rājastambāyana;
Yajñavacas Rājastambāyana from Tura Kāvaṣeya; Tura Kāvaṣeya from Prajāpati; and Prajāpati from Brahman.
Salutation to Brahmā, the self-existent, to Brahmā.
